title: Week 1: your first options lesson
body:
# Week 1: your first options lesson

**Goal:** understand what a listed option is, what one contract can cost or obligate you to do, and why a favorable stock move does not guarantee a profit. First read the opening lesson in [Volume 1, Module 1](LESSONS_01_FOUNDATIONS.md) for stocks, ETFs, indexes, and brokers. Try the short diagnostic in [the practical math bridge](FOUNDATION_MATH_BRIDGE.md); use its lessons alongside this week if percentages or algebra are new. This week is study and observation only.

## The simplest mental model

A **stock** is an ownership interest. An **option** is a time-limited contract tied to an underlying asset. This first lesson uses **standard, physically settled stock options**: a **call** gives its buyer the right to buy shares at a stated **strike price**; a **put** gives its buyer the right to sell shares at the strike. The buyer pays a **premium**. The seller receives the premium and takes the corresponding obligation if assigned. Standard U.S. listed equity options generally deliver 100 shares, but check each contract's **premium multiplier** and **exercise deliverable** separately, especially after an adjustment. The [SEC's stock-options introduction](https://www.investor.gov/introduction-investing/general-resources/news-alerts/alerts-bulletins/investor-bulletins-63) is the reference for these basics. Some index options instead [settle in cash](https://www.optionseducation.org/advancedconcepts/equity-vs-index-options); they do not deliver shares.

An option has an **expiration date**. Its price before expiration responds to the underlying price, time remaining, expected volatility, rates, dividends, and market supply and demand. The payoff arithmetic below applies **at expiration**. Before then, the market price can be different from its intrinsic value.

### Example 1: buying a call

Assume a stock is at $100. You buy one call with a $105 strike for a quoted premium of $3.00 per share. Assume a 100-share multiplier and ignore fees for this exercise.

- Up-front cost: **$3 × 100 = $300**.
- At expiration, if the stock is $112, the call's intrinsic value is **($112 − $105) × 100 = $700**. Profit is **$700 − $300 = $400**.
- At expiration, if the stock is $106, the call is worth $100, yet your profit is **$100 − $300 = −$200**. The stock went up, but not enough to cover the premium.
- If the stock finishes at or below $105, the call expires without intrinsic value and the full **$300** premium is lost.
- Expiration break-even stock price: **$105 + $3 = $108**, before fees.

The long-call expiration-profit formula is `multiplier × max(stock price − strike, 0) − multiplier × premium − fees`.

### Example 2: buying a put

Assume the same stock is at $100. You buy one $95-strike put for $2.00 per share, again with a 100-share multiplier and no fees.

- Cost: **$200**.
- At expiration, with the stock at $88, intrinsic value is **($95 − $88) × 100 = $700**. Profit is **$500**.
- Expiration break-even stock price: **$95 − $2 = $93**.
- At or above $95 at expiration, the full $200 premium is lost.

The long-put expiration-profit formula is `multiplier × max(strike − stock price, 0) − multiplier × premium − fees`.

### The other side has obligations

If you **sell** a call without owning the shares or another offsetting position, you may have to deliver shares at the strike even when the market price is much higher. A stock has no fixed upper price limit, so the uncovered short call's theoretical loss is unlimited. A short put can require buying the shares at the strike after they have fallen substantially. Premium received is payment for taking risk, not a guaranteed income stream. See the [SEC risk explanation](https://www.investor.gov/introduction-investing/general-resources/news-alerts/alerts-bulletins/investor-bulletins-63) and the [OCC disclosure document](https://www.theocc.com/company-information/documents-and-archives/options-disclosure-document).

An apparently limited-risk spread can still produce a temporary stock position if its short American-style option is assigned and its other leg remains open. The exact outcome depends on the contract and your broker's procedures. You will rehearse this before simulation in [RISK_AND_OPERATIONS.md](RISK_AND_OPERATIONS.md).

### The cost hidden in a quote

Suppose an option is quoted **$2.10 bid / $2.30 ask**. Buying one at the ask costs $230. Selling it immediately at the bid brings back $210, a **$20 loss before commissions**. The $2.20 midpoint is a calculation, not a promised fill. Options with wide spreads can turn an attractive payoff into a poor trade. See [Cboe's liquidity explanation](https://optionsfacts.cboe.com/).

## Your 10-hour plan

| Day | Time | Task |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| 1 | 1 h | Read the SEC introduction through terminology. Write your own definitions of stock, call, put, strike, premium, multiplier, expiration. |
| 2 | 1.5 h | Work Example 1 again without looking; draw its profit at stock prices $90, $100, $105, $108, $112, $120. If needed, practice units and percentages in [the math bridge](FOUNDATION_MATH_BRIDGE.md) and verify the drawing with its short Python example after solving by hand. |
| 3 | 1.5 h | Work Example 2 again; draw its profit at $80, $88, $93, $95, $100, $110. |
| 4 | 1.5 h | Read the SEC's risk section, then use the guided questions below while reading the stock-option definitions in Chapter I and holder/writer risks in Chapter X of the [OCC disclosure document](https://www.theocc.com/company-information/documents-and-archives/options-disclosure-document). Bookmark any unfinished section for weeks 13 and 21. |
| 5 | 1.5 h | Look at a delayed option chain using [OIC's tools](https://www.optionseducation.org/Options-Quotes-Calculators). Record the date, underlying, expiration, strike, call/put, premium multiplier, exercise deliverable, bid, ask, and source. If a field is missing, mark it unknown and consult the contract specification. Calculate one-contract bid/ask cost only when its multiplier is known. Do not place an order. |
| 6 | 2 h | Start [OIC Options 101](https://prd-web.optionseducation.org/theoptionseducationcenter/occ-learning). Correct your definitions and payoff drawings. |
| 7 | 1 h | Take all ten questions below without notes, then complete the two [new-number transfer cases](FOUNDATION_ASSESSMENTS.md) before reading their separate key. Write three questions you still have. |

### Guided questions for Day 4

As you read, write one sentence for each: (1) What right does a call or put holder receive? (2) What can an assigned writer have to deliver or buy? (3) When can a buyer lose the full premium? (4) Why can a writer lose more than the premium collected? (5) What cash or shares might be needed if one leg of a stock-option spread is assigned? Highlight unfamiliar terms and revisit them in Modules 4 and 6. The [OCC disclosure](https://www.theocc.com/company-information/documents-and-archives/options-disclosure-document) is a reference to learn over time; finish any longer reading after this introductory session.

## Check yourself

Use a 100-share multiplier and ignore fees for questions 4–8. Answer before opening the key.

1. For a standard stock call, what right does the buyer have? What obligation can the seller have?
2. For a standard stock put, what right does the buyer have? What obligation can the seller have?
3. Which contract details must you confirm before computing its dollar size?
4. You buy one $105 call for $3. What is your maximum premium loss, and your expiration break-even stock price?
5. The call in question 4 expires with the stock at $112. What is its profit?
6. You buy one $95 put for $2. The stock ends at $88. What is its profit?
7. You buy an option at a $2.30 ask and immediately sell at a $2.10 bid. What is the result before fees?
8. A stock rises from $100 to $106 by expiration. Did the $105 call bought for $3 earn a profit? Why?
9. Does a high option premium guarantee an option seller a profit?
10. Can a short American-style option be assigned before expiration?

<details>
<summary>Answer key</summary>

1. The buyer can buy the shares at the strike under the contract terms; an assigned seller must deliver them.
2. The buyer can sell the shares at the strike; an assigned seller must buy them.
3. At least the underlying, call or put type, strike, expiration, premium multiplier, and exercise deliverable as separate fields; also confirm any adjustment and settlement details before acting.
4. $300 premium loss; $108 expiration break-even, before fees.
5. $400 profit.
6. $500 profit.
7. A $20 loss before fees.
8. No. Its $100 intrinsic value is less than the $300 premium; profit is −$200 before fees.
9. No. Losses can exceed premium collected and may be very large.
10. Yes. Check product style and your broker's procedures; [OIC explains exercise and assignment](https://www.optionseducation.org/optionsoverview/exercising-options).

</details>

**Pass standard:** Correct **all ten** questions and explain the rights, obligations, and arithmetic in plain language. Complete the two [new-number transfer cases](FOUNDATION_ASSESSMENTS.md) before checking [their separate answers](FOUNDATION_ANSWER_KEY.md). Rework any error with changed numbers, then continue Sprint 1 in [COURSE.md](COURSE.md).

title: How to take this course
body:
# How to take this course

This course assumes **no trading background**. Start with [Volume 1, Module 1](LESSONS_01_FOUNDATIONS.md), which explains stocks and markets, then complete [the first seven days](ADVANCED_FIRST_WEEK.md) as its first practice week. Continue the teaching volumes in order. [COURSE.md](COURSE.md) is the map; the **lesson volumes** contain the explanations and exercises. Most weeks have ten hours of work. If a topic takes longer, stay with it.

Before assigning later weeks, take the [arithmetic and math diagnostic](FOUNDATION_MATH_BRIDGE.md) and record the first attempt in a copy of [the learning record](LEARNING_RECORD_TEMPLATE.md). A learner who already codes can bring Python into the first payoff lesson and demonstrate Module 15's programming skill early. Use the saved study time for options, probability, and contract arithmetic. Programming experience never substitutes for those gates. The [three goal paths](MASTERY_TRACKS.md) become projects after the common core; you may pursue all three in sequence.

## The learning loop

1. **Learn one idea.** Read one section of the current lesson and say it back in ordinary language. If a term cannot be explained without using three more unfamiliar terms, pause and look it up.
2. **Work an example by hand.** Cover the worked solution. Write the input, units, formula or reasoning, result, and what the result means. Use dollars, shares, contracts, percentage points, and dates explicitly.
3. **Change one assumption.** For a payoff example, change the stock price or premium. For a research example, change the fee or fill. Ask whether the conclusion survives.
4. **Attempt exercises before the key.** Record an answer even if uncertain. Then check the separate solution and write the exact step you missed. Re-solve a fresh problem a day later without the key. Use the [foundation assessment bank](FOUNDATION_ASSESSMENTS.md) for unfamiliar cases.
5. **Build the module artifact.** A chart, ledger, memo, or case analysis is evidence of skill. Watching the videos is only preparation.
6. **Pass the gate.** The numerical result and the explanation must both be right. Safety-critical mistakes about contract size, cash obligations, assignment, and settlement require a new correct attempt before progressing. Preserve the prompt, original answer, correction, and retest in [the learning record](LEARNING_RECORD_TEMPLATE.md).

An option may be complex without being mysterious. Draw its cash flows, ask what can happen before expiration, and check the exact contract terms. The current [OCC disclosure document](https://www.theocc.com/company-information/documents-and-archives/options-disclosure-document) and broker procedures are references whenever the case concerns a real product.

## Use me as your tutor

You can work through the material in this chat. Ask **“Teach me Week 1, Day 1”** and I should explain one concept at a time, show a simple example, ask you to solve a new example, and respond to your reasoning. When you are ready, ask **“Quiz me on Module 1 without showing answers.”** Send your answers; I should mark each one, explain misses, and give fresh cases before advancing. Ask **“Review my module artifact”** to get feedback against its pass gate.

Do not copy an answer key into your response to pass a gate. Being able to solve an unseen version matters more than remembering a number. The answer key is for feedback, not a score to collect.

For a deeper review, ask **“Give me a fresh assignment case with an account balance and broker deadline; wait for my full ledger.”** For research, ask **“Challenge the timing, costs, and benchmark of my dated protocol.”** Record the answers and changes in your own files; a chat response by itself is not an enduring research record.

## Weekly record

Use [the full learning record template](LEARNING_RECORD_TEMPLATE.md) for assessment attempts, artifacts, and gate decisions. At minimum, copy this block into a dated journal file each week:

```text
Week / module:
Hours studied (target 10; actual):
Concepts I can explain without notes:
Worked examples attempted:
Exercises correct on first attempt:
Fresh retest attempted, identifier, and result:
Errors and corrected reasoning:
One option-chain or market observation, with source and timestamp:
What I still do not understand:
Module artifact progress:
Artifact file path, input version, and independent check:
Any paper decision and its prewritten reason (later modules only):
Any no-trade decision or unfilled order (later modules only):
Next week's focus:
```

For market observations, a delayed quote is suitable for learning but not a promise of an executable price. Record the displayed bid and ask, not only the midpoint. [OIC labels its tool data as delayed](https://www.optionseducation.org/options-quotes-calculators).

## Advancement record

| Module | Lesson read and taught back | Exercises attempted before key | Artifact complete | Gate passed | Date |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Money and markets |  |  |  |  |  |
| 2. Reading quotes |  |  |  |  |  |
| 3. Calls and puts |  |  |  |  |  |
| 4. Contract lifecycle |  |  |  |  |  |
| 5. Position structures |  |  |  |  |  |
| 6. First risk exam |  |  |  |  |  |
| 7. Greeks |  |  |  |  |  |
| 8. Volatility |  |  |  |  |  |
| 9. Greek combinations |  |  |  |  |  |
| 10. Trade design |  |  |  |  |  |
| 11. Execution |  |  |  |  |  |
| 12. Simulation |  |  |  |  |  |
| 13. Probability |  |  |  |  |  |
| 14. Statistics |  |  |  |  |  |
| 15. Python |  |  |  |  |  |
| 16. Data quality |  |  |  |  |  |
| 17. Pricing logic |  |  |  |  |  |
| 18. Black–Scholes |  |  |  |  |  |
| 19. Volatility surface |  |  |  |  |  |
| 20. Sources of return |  |  |  |  |  |
| 21. Research protocol |  |  |  |  |  |
| 22. Historical test |  |  |  |  |  |
| 23. Robustness |  |  |  |  |  |
| 24. Portfolio risk |  |  |  |  |  |
| 25. Specialization |  |  |  |  |  |
| 26. Independent audit |  |  |  |  |  |

Each row is an index to dated evidence, not a self-awarded certificate. Record first-attempt errors and later fresh retests in [the learning record](LEARNING_RECORD_TEMPLATE.md). Repeated work is expected. A passed quiz does not mean a strategy is profitable, and simulation does not prove live results. The [risk guide](RISK_AND_OPERATIONS.md) defines the operational gates before any live decision.

## Reading order

1. [LESSONS_01_FOUNDATIONS.md](LESSONS_01_FOUNDATIONS.md): read Module 1's lesson first, then continue Modules 1–6.
2. [ADVANCED_FIRST_WEEK.md](ADVANCED_FIRST_WEEK.md): Module 1's first seven days, after its opening lesson.
3. [LESSONS_02_BEHAVIOR.md](LESSONS_02_BEHAVIOR.md): modules 7–12.
4. [LESSONS_03_QUANT.md](LESSONS_03_QUANT.md): modules 13–18.
5. [LESSONS_04_RESEARCH.md](LESSONS_04_RESEARCH.md): modules 19–26.
6. [FOUNDATION_MATH_BRIDGE.md](FOUNDATION_MATH_BRIDGE.md) runs alongside the first modules. [FOUNDATION_ASSESSMENTS.md](FOUNDATION_ASSESSMENTS.md) and its [separate key](FOUNDATION_ANSWER_KEY.md) supply unfamiliar foundation cases.
7. [OPERATIONAL_CASEBOOK.md](OPERATIONAL_CASEBOOK.md), [EXECUTION_PRACTICE.md](EXECUTION_PRACTICE.md), and [DYNAMIC_HEDGING_LAB.md](DYNAMIC_HEDGING_LAB.md) rehearse account, order, and hedge decisions before or during simulation.
8. [labs/README.md](labs/README.md) runs the coding apprenticeship, from payoff arithmetic to a research report. [LEARNING_RECORD_TEMPLATE.md](LEARNING_RECORD_TEMPLATE.md) preserves evidence; [MASTERY_TRACKS.md](MASTERY_TRACKS.md) defines the three later paths.
9. [SOURCES.md](SOURCES.md), [RISK_AND_OPERATIONS.md](RISK_AND_OPERATIONS.md), and [RESEARCH_LAB.md](RESEARCH_LAB.md) are references throughout.

title: Optional advanced track: the 104-week options curriculum
body:
# Optional advanced track: the 104-week options curriculum

**Start with the [beginner microcourse](beginner/README.md) at 10–15 minutes per study day.** This longer map is an optional reference and advanced study path. Its quantitative programming, pricing, and research modules are not prerequisites for beginning the microcourse, understanding options, choosing not to trade, or considering personal suitability. Completing either path does not approve anyone for live trading.

**Audience:** learners choosing deeper study, with an early Python path for those who already code. **Market:** U.S. listed options. **Optional pace:** 10 hours per week for 104 weeks (about 1,040 hours). **Outcome:** a core within this advanced path in contracts, risk, execution, mathematics, and research, followed by [personal portfolio, independent research, or professional quant paths](MASTERY_TRACKS.md). The timeline extends when prerequisites or gates need more work. World-class performance cannot be promised by a syllabus and would require continued evidence over years and market regimes.

The sequence is intentionally cumulative. A person who knows many strategy names but cannot explain assignment, identify bad data, or measure costs is not ready to take risk.

## How to study each week

| Activity | Hours | Evidence to keep |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| Read or watch one primary lesson | 2 | Notes in your own words; three questions |
| Solve problems or build a small tool | 3 | Worked answers, code, or diagrams |
| Observe real option chains and product specifications | 2 | Dated observations; no need to trade |
| Write a journal or research memo | 2 | Decision, uncertainty, what would change your mind |
| Recall quiz and review errors | 1 | Corrected mistakes and next action |

Once simulation begins, replace some observation time with carefully selected paper decisions. A simulator is a teaching tool; its fills can differ from live fills. [IBKR documents several paper trading limitations](https://www.ibkrguides.com/orgportal/aboutpapertradingaccount.htm).

**Advancement rule:** Complete the sprint artifact and meet its pass standard before starting the next sprint. For ordinary concepts, aim for at least 90% on a closed-note recall quiz and correct any misses. For contract size, maximum loss, exercise, assignment, settlement, and margin questions, require 100% accuracy in fresh scenarios. Rework mistakes; time spent repeating a sprint is productive. The eight-week paper-decision record is the one planned overlap: its later weeks may run alongside Modules 13–14, but Risk Gate 2 remains open until every requirement is met.

Begin with the diagnostic in [the foundation math bridge](FOUNDATION_MATH_BRIDGE.md). Keep original answers, corrections, later fresh retests, code versions, and reviewer decisions in [the learning record](LEARNING_RECORD_TEMPLATE.md). If you already know Python, demonstrate it with a small clean-data and hand-check exercise, then use programming for early payoff and data labs. You may replace Module 15's introductory syntax work with a more demanding artifact, but its reproducibility gate still applies. No diagnostic bypasses the contract or safety exams.

## Stage 1 — financial and options literacy (weeks 1–24)

The full explanations, worked examples, weekly plans, and answer keys are in [Teaching Volume 1](LESSONS_01_FOUNDATIONS.md).

Read the opening lesson in [Volume 1, Module 1](LESSONS_01_FOUNDATIONS.md), then complete [the seven-day introduction](ADVANCED_FIRST_WEEK.md). Practice percentages, units, and break-even algebra with the [math bridge](FOUNDATION_MATH_BRIDGE.md). Use [the separate foundation assessment bank](FOUNDATION_ASSESSMENTS.md) and [answer key](FOUNDATION_ANSWER_KEY.md) for fresh cases. Use the free [SEC introduction](https://www.investor.gov/introduction-investing/general-resources/news-alerts/alerts-bulletins/investor-bulletins-63), [OIC Options Academy](https://prd-web.optionseducation.org/theoptionseducationcenter/occ-learning), and [Cboe Options Institute](https://www.cboe.com/optionsinstitute/learningportal/). Read the current [OCC options disclosure document](https://www.theocc.com/company-information/documents-and-archives/options-disclosure-document) before any simulation of a strategy and again before any live trading.

| Sprint | Weeks | Learn and practice | Required artifact and pass standard |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Money and markets | 1–4 | Saving versus trading; stocks, ETFs, indexes; returns, compounding, drawdowns; percentages and dollar units; what an exchange, broker, and clearinghouse do. | One-page learning plan and the 12 core terms in [Module 1](LESSONS_01_FOUNDATIONS.md), explained without copying definitions. Complete the math diagnostic and explain why a 50% drawdown needs a 100% gain to recover. Grow the glossary across Stage 1. |
| 2. Reading the market | 5–8 | Bid, ask, spread, last, volume, open interest, order types, multiplier, expiration, corporate action calendar. | Annotate 20 real but *untraded* option chain quotes, with timestamp and source. Compute the round-trip spread cost of each at displayed bid/ask. |
| 3. Calls and puts | 9–12 | Rights versus obligations; long/short calls and puts; intrinsic and extrinsic value; expiration payoff and breakeven. | Hand-solve and graph 40 cases from the [fresh assessment bank](FOUNDATION_ASSESSMENTS.md), including fees, then check against its separate key. Correct every multiplier and worst-case mistake with a new case. Verify selected results with code after doing them by hand. |
| 4. Contract lifecycle | 13–16 | Exercise, early assignment, expiration, ex-dividend risk, adjusted contracts, account permissions, ODD. | Complete the [operational casebook](OPERATIONAL_CASEBOOK.md) and a fresh scenario exam: short call assigned early, short put assigned, spread with one leg assigned, expiration near strike, and cash-settled index option. Reconcile resulting positions, multiplier, deliverable, and cash obligations. |
| 5. Position structures | 17–20 | Stock plus options; protective puts, covered calls, cash-secured puts, verticals, straddles, strangles, butterflies, and iron condors. Separate expiration payoff from path and operational risk. | Build a payoff notebook with 12 same-expiration structures. For each, show net debit/credit, idealized expiration payoff, qualitative stock-price/time/volatility exposure, assignment exposure, and a case where the trade disappoints. |
| 6. First risk exam | 21–24 | Concentration, defined versus undefined risk, leverage, gap risk, liquidity, margin, taxes and recordkeeping. | Complete the [risk guide](RISK_AND_OPERATIONS.md), the [unseen safety assessment](FOUNDATION_ASSESSMENTS.md), and full cash/position cases from the [operational casebook](OPERATIONAL_CASEBOOK.md). Pass all safety cases after remediation. Remain in observation mode until passed. |

**Gate A:** Explain an option quote, draw the four basic payoffs, distinguish a right from an obligation, compute contract dollar amounts, and handle assignment/settlement cases without help. Maintain at least 40 accurately explained terms accumulated across Stage 1. No live trades.

## Stage 2 — how option prices and trades behave (weeks 25–48)

Study [Teaching Volume 2](LESSONS_02_BEHAVIOR.md) alongside this map.

Use [OIC Greeks and volatility modules](https://prd-web.optionseducation.org/theoptionseducationcenter/occ-learning), [IBKR's recommended options course sequence](https://www.interactivebrokers.com/campus/traders-academy/finance-courses/), and [OIC's delayed calculators](https://www.optionseducation.org/Options-Quotes-Calculators). A calculator checks work; it does not replace explanation.

| Sprint | Weeks | Learn and practice | Required artifact and pass standard |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 7. Greeks I | 25–28 | Delta, gamma, theta, vega, rho; local approximations and why they break on large moves. | Predict the direction of price changes in 30 stock/IV/time/rate scenarios, then compare with a calculator and explain errors. |
| 8. Volatility I | 29–32 | Realized versus implied volatility, annualization, event volatility, skew, term structure; IV rank versus percentile. | A weekly volatility diary for two underlyings. State what each measure says and what it does *not* prove about value or future profit. |
| 9. Greek combinations | 33–36 | Net position Greeks, nonlinear exposure, volatility crush, calendars and term structure, delta hedging concept, correlation risk. | Five scenario matrices for multi-leg positions over changes in price, IV, and days to expiry, plus the [discrete hedge ledger](DYNAMIC_HEDGING_LAB.md). Include a calendar, which still has a live long leg when its short leg expires; reconcile the hedge cash and residual exposure. |
| 10. Trade design | 37–40 | Thesis, time horizon, alternatives, target exposure, rejection criteria, event calendar. | Write 10 hypothetical trade tickets and 10 explicit no-trade decisions. Each ticket must say why stock or cash is not a better expression. |
| 11. Execution | 41–44 | NBBO, spread, depth, limit orders, complex orders, fees, partial fills, slippage, exit liquidity. | Observe 30 option quote changes and complete the [timestamped execution replay](EXECUTION_PRACTICE.md). Record order intent, nonfills, cancellations, conservative entry/exit estimates, and uncertainty about queue position; do not assume midpoint fills. |
| 12. Simulation and review | 45–48 | Simulator setup, written pretrade plan, journal, error taxonomy, weekly review, benchmark. | Begin the eight-week paper-decision record specified by [Risk Gate 2](RISK_AND_OPERATIONS.md). Log every eligible setup, pass, failed order, costs, drawdown, and rule violation. Continue the record alongside Modules 13–14 until eight weeks and the gate conditions are met; no forced trade count. |

**Gate B:** Show that you can analyze a trade before entry, identify its costs and exposures, complete the execution replay, and record every decision. The four-week Module 12 artifact is an interim review; [Risk Gate 2](RISK_AND_OPERATIONS.md) still requires at least eight weeks and its full decision record before it can pass. Paper profits do not pass either gate by themselves.

## Stage 3 — quantitative foundation (weeks 49–72)

Study [Teaching Volume 3](LESSONS_03_QUANT.md) alongside this map.

No coding experience is assumed. Start statistics with [Khan Academy's Statistics and Probability](https://www.khanacademy.org/math/statistics-probability) and programming with [MIT's introductory Python course](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-100l-introduction-to-cs-and-programming-using-python-fall-2022/), which is designed for little or no programming experience. Learners who already code can use the [lab sequence](labs/README.md) from the beginning and challenge the syntax portion of Module 15. Use the [official Python tutorial](https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/) later as a reference; it assumes prior programming knowledge. If algebra and functions are new, begin with the [math bridge](FOUNDATION_MATH_BRIDGE.md) and [Khan Academy's algebra basics](https://www.khanacademy.org/mission/algebra-basics) and extend the timeline. [MIT 18.05](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-05-introduction-to-probability-and-statistics-spring-2022/pages/syllabus/) lists multivariable calculus as a prerequisite; use its deeper problems after the needed calculus. [MIT Analytics of Finance](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/15-450-analytics-of-finance-fall-2010/pages/syllabus/) is a later graduate-level extension, not an entry course. The 104-week schedule is a target, not a reason to skip prerequisites.

| Sprint | Weeks | Learn and practice | Required artifact and pass standard |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 13. Probability | 49–52 | Conditional probability, distributions, expectation, variance, tail events, expected value versus win rate. | Complete the relevant Khan Academy unit tests and worked examples. Explain why a 90% win rate can still lose money and why a model probability is not a promise. |
| 14. Statistical inference | 53–56 | Sampling error, confidence intervals, hypothesis tests, autocorrelation, selection bias, multiple comparisons. | Complete the relevant Khan inference units, critique three claimed trading edges, and work the [dependent-observation and trial-log lab](labs/README.md). Identify costs, sample selection, hidden tests, and an unseen period. Continue the paper record if Risk Gate 2 is still open. |
| 15. Python for analysis | 57–60 | New programmers begin with MIT introductory Python; experienced programmers demonstrate data validation, tests, plotting, saved inputs, and reproducible calculations. | A clean-run script that loads a price series, computes returns and realized volatility, plots both, and reproduces the hand-checked results. Experienced programmers replace syntax exercises with a tested [lab artifact](labs/README.md); everyone passes the same reproducibility gate. |
| 16. Data quality | 61–64 | Option identifiers, splits/adjustments, missing quotes, stale markets, survivorship, time zones, corporate actions, point-in-time data. | A data dictionary and QA report. Reject impossible observations; flag and investigate crossed, stale, and zero-bid conditions under prespecified rules. A real zero bid can signal illiquidity. Document every filter without peeking at future outcomes, and preserve held positions and unresolved exits. |
| 17. Pricing logic | 65–68 | No arbitrage, put-call parity, binomial replication, American versus European exercise. | Price simple options with a small binomial tree; show the replicating logic and test parity on idealized examples. |
| 18. Black–Scholes and limits | 69–72 | Model assumptions, implied volatility inversion, Greeks by calculation, dividends, volatility smiles, model error. | Implement or inspect a European option pricer and compare numerical Greeks with finite differences. Explain at least five ways real products depart from its assumptions. |

**Gate C:** Reproduce calculations from raw inputs, state model assumptions, and identify bad data. Study of stochastic calculus is optional until this foundation is firm; the professional extension is [MIT 15.450](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/15-450-analytics-of-finance-fall-2010/pages/lecture-notes/).

## Stage 4 — research, portfolio risk, and specialization (weeks 73–104)

Study [Teaching Volume 4](LESSONS_04_RESEARCH.md) alongside this map.

The [research lab](RESEARCH_LAB.md) supplies full protocols and templates; the [runnable labs](labs/README.md) supply small synthetic inputs and checks. Research questions must be stated before examining the final test outcomes. An apparently profitable options strategy must survive realistic spreads, commissions, assignment/settlement assumptions, an untouched later period, and a fair benchmark. Published research on [backtest overfitting](https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2326253) and [option premia changing within the authors' historical sample](https://www.nber.org/papers/w31833) motivates this discipline.

| Sprint | Weeks | Learn and practice | Required artifact and pass standard |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 19. Volatility surface | 73–76 | Moneyness, tenor, skew, smile, forward volatility, surface dynamics, calendar/butterfly arbitrage checks. | Plot dated surface slices and write five observations and five data/model caveats. Check strike monotonicity/convexity and solve the qualified two-expiry calendar case in Volume 4, including its cash/share ledger and fresh transfer question. |
| 20. Sources of return | 77–80 | Direction, volatility risk premium, insurance demand, event risk, carry, convexity, hedging costs, competition. | A literature memo comparing three explanations for one proposed edge, with at least one reason the edge could disappear. |
| 21. Research protocol | 81–84 | Define a falsifiable hypothesis, population, contract selector, entry/exit, benchmark, costs, risk, and stopping rule. Check data access, fields, license, timestamp resolution, and budget before finalizing the question. | Pre-register one question and comparator using [the research template](RESEARCH_LAB.md); select an honest evidence level—synthetic system validation, published-index analysis, or licensed historical-contract replay—before looking at results. |
| 22. Historical test or declared alternative | 85–88 | Point-in-time replay, quote-side fills, commissions, corporate actions, assignment, position limits, and the limits of available data. | Reproduce the chosen evidence-level project with a trade, simulation, or published-observation record as appropriate, data QA, sensitivity, and independent checks. A synthetic test validates software; published-index history supports an index comparison; contract-level claims require suitable contract quotes. Begin forward shadow logging where the protocol produces live-observable decisions. |
| 23. Robustness | 89–92 | Chronological holdout where genuinely possible, regime splits, sensitivity, and a complete trial log; for contract-level studies, walk-forward checks and trade dependence. | Report all tried variants and failed results. Reserve a final segment before viewing it when feasible; an already examined public index series remains descriptive. A tests unseen synthetic cases; B tests published-series comparisons and methodology sensitivity; C tests the historical contract rule and continues its forward shadow log. |
| 24. Portfolio risk | 93–96 | Aggregate Greeks, correlated moves, gap/IV/liquidity shocks, margin, concentration, and drawdowns on a hypothetical portfolio. | Stress at least eight joint scenarios using stated contract assumptions and a funding ledger. A can use a synthetic fixture; B's separate published-index study cannot supply constituent contract cash obligations, so add a clearly labeled hypothetical portfolio exercise; C also stresses actual study positions and continues forward logging. |
| 25. Specialization | 97–100 | Use the [three goal paths](MASTERY_TRACKS.md) to choose one current project; within it, investigate hedging/overlay, volatility relative value, event options, systematic index strategies, market microstructure, or options on futures. | Produce a critical review and feasible small test or simulation. Explain its needed mathematics, data, technology, capital, and expertise. Continue the appropriate A/B/C evidence record. |
| 26. Independent audit | 101–104 | Reconcile the selected A/B/C evidence record, comparator, costs or index assumptions, exceptions, and risk; present a research defense. | A level-labeled capstone report and reproducible evidence bundle. Include failed ideas and uncertainty. Have another knowledgeable person challenge assumptions before treating any edge as established. |

**Gate D:** The capstone has a complete decision, simulation, or published-observation record appropriate to its data; an explicit treatment of costs and source assumptions; no obvious future-data leakage; a frozen question and later evaluation where the data permit one; a fair comparator; stress or sensitivity results; and a candid statement of uncertainty. Label its evidence level. A synthetic simulation can pass a software/accounting audit but cannot establish a market edge. A published index comparison does not prove its constituent option trades were replicated. A negative or inconclusive result can pass; concealing a failed test cannot.

## Before considering live capital

The course does not automatically graduate anyone to live trading. Gates A–D are completion standards for this optional advanced research path, rather than universal or regulatory prerequisites for every personal investment decision. A separate live-capital decision requires understanding the intended position and its obligations, reading the current ODD, confirming broker permissions and exact product specifications, considering personal finances and an affordable loss limit, and rehearsing assignment/expiry and order handling. **A synthetic level-A capstone shows that a simulator follows its rules; it does not supply evidence that a live strategy has an edge.** Claims about a strategy's edge need suitable real-market evidence, realistic execution assumptions, and forward observations. Simulated fills and small samples cannot prove an edge. Choosing to remain in observation or simulation is a valid outcome. The extended [risk guide](RISK_AND_OPERATIONS.md) describes an illustrative training policy; personal and broker requirements remain separate from course grades.

The 2026 FINRA intraday margin changes have a broker transition period. Verify the rule your broker actually applies rather than relying on an old universal pattern-day-trader summary. See [FINRA's current explanation](https://www.finra.org/investors/insights/intraday-margin-requirements).

## Beyond the core: the multi-year mastery loop

Repeat a disciplined cycle: identify a narrow question; read primary research; make a testable forecast; build point-in-time data; compare with a simple alternative; forward test; cap risk; independently audit; and retire ideas when evidence changes. Over several market regimes, measure **net** returns, drawdowns, tail losses, capacity, execution quality, tax/operational drag, and decision quality. Exceptional trading is an evidence claim, not a certificate or a trade count.

Optional advanced study: [MIT's finance mathematics course](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-642-topics-in-mathematics-with-applications-in-finance-fall-2024/), [MIT Analytics of Finance](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/15-450-analytics-of-finance-fall-2010/pages/syllabus/), and the publisher-verified books in [SOURCES.md](SOURCES.md). Buy books or historical option data only when a specific project needs them.

After the common core, use [the three path standards](MASTERY_TRACKS.md) for personal portfolio decisions, independent trading research, and professional quant preparation. They require different evidence and may take several additional years. Keep one advanced project active long enough to defend it before changing focus.

title: Course technical audit — November 14, 2026
body:
# Course technical audit — November 14, 2026

This is an AI-assisted technical audit and remediation record. It does not claim human expert credentials, external approval, completed learner participation or demonstrated teaching effectiveness. The original reports and portable reproduction script are preserved under `audit/2026-11-14/`. This snapshot includes original findings and their verified closures.


## Quantitative course validation — November 14, 2026

This is an **AI-assisted independent technical audit** of the current source, performed with separately derived formulas and numerical references. It is not a human expert review, academic accreditation, a learner pilot, or evidence of learning gains. No learner responses, reviewer approvals, retention outcomes, or market performance were generated by this audit.

### Scope and result

Reviewed all 26 original case briefs, exhibits, updates and debriefs in `course-app/content/graduate.json`, every question family in `course-app/lib/graduate-practice.ts`, and the pure calculations in `graduate-models.ts` and `portfolio-research-models.ts`.

**3,724 numerical assertions passed:** 3,626 program/reference comparisons and 98 independently recomputed case relationships. There were no failed arithmetic assertions within the sampled domain. The review identified two assessment-wording defects and a public-helper boundary limitation below; these are distinct from incorrect answer keys.

Evidence files:

- `audit/2026-11-14/reproduce-quantitative-validation.py` — repeatable audit script; uses a separate Python `math.erf` normal CDF and independently expressed cash/payoff/statistical equations.
- `audit/2026-11-14/quantitative-validation-results.json` — exact grid counts, maximum differences and case results.

Run the script with Python 3 and the app's supported Node runtime. It locates the workspace from its own path, so it can be run after moving the checkout.

### Independent checks performed

| Area | Coverage actually executed | Result |
|---|---|---|
| European prices | 2,430 parameter combinations: five spots, three strikes, three maturities, three volatilities, three rates, three dividend yields, call and put | All within $0.01/share of independent Python Black–Scholes reference. Maximum absolute difference $0.00247078/share. |
| Numerical Greeks | 432 parameter combinations; 1,728 comparisons with analytic delta/gamma/vega and independently repriced one-day time change | Differences measured, not represented as exact derivative agreement. See precision observations. |
| Practice answer keys | 780 numeric keys: all 26 modules × 3 questions × ten sequences, including 0/1, modulus boundaries and 1,000,000 | All agreed with independently derived answers within $0.001 or the corresponding question unit. |
| Common-budget strategy comparison | 21 scenarios × four alternatives × cash/wealth/P&L | 252 assertions passed. Opening fees and retained cash reconciled. |
| Short-call assignment | 15 stock/long-mark combinations | 45 assertions passed for cash, short shares, surviving long call, equity and alternative gross cash actions. |
| Execution replay | Seven limits spanning no fill, one fill and two fills | 14 assertions passed for positions, cash, average fill and acknowledged final cancellation. |
| Research critique | 32 packets covering all 16 issue combinations twice | 96 assertions passed for diagnosis, net result and benchmark difference. |
| Joint portfolio stress | Independent signed delta/gamma/vega aggregation and separate funding ledger | Nine assertions passed. Local equity $47,463.04; after supplied exit cost $47,213.04; immediate cash shortfall $750. |
| Original case arithmetic | 98 checks across the 23 modules with scalar calculations | All passed. The other three cases were reviewed as evidence/interpretation cases rather than assigned artificial numerical passes. |

The 98 case checks include all 20 cells of the flagship portfolio table, initial and revised hedge cash, floor/cap and underlying-zero boundary; the 90% win-rate example and joint loss; multiple-testing illustration; replication; convexity and executable package cost; omitted-exit accounting; aggregate spread funding; and the capstone's cost convention and drawdown. The corrected actual-fill capstone convention yields $1,900 project net if the $700 slippage was already embedded, subject to verifying the supplied report.

### Findings reported for correction

| ID | Severity | Location | Finding and recommended correction |
|---|---|---|---|
| QV-01 | Low, teaching wording | `course-app/lib/graduate-practice.ts:15` | The prompt says the account “rises” on odd sequences even though the final balance is lower. Replace with “changes from” so the signed-return task does not contradict its data. Arithmetic keys are correct. |
| QV-02 | Moderate, conceptual ambiguity | `course-app/lib/graduate-practice.ts:29` | Question 1 explicitly evaluates expiration; Question 2 refers to “the same” option with positive extrinsic value and calls the quote coherent. Specify a separate **before-expiration snapshot** in Question 2. Otherwise the sequence can teach time value at expiration. Arithmetic decomposition is correct for the intended earlier snapshot. |
| QV-03 | Low, helper-domain boundary | `course-app/lib/graduate-models.ts:24` | `europeanPrice` accepts volatility 5 and spot 10,000,000, but `europeanSensitivities` bumps those values beyond the validated domain and throws. Current UI limits of 200% volatility and $10,000 spot avoid this. Either explicitly restrict the sensitivity-helper domain or use qualified boundary differences; do not describe the pricer's entire domain as its derivative-helper domain. |

These findings were sent to the implementation owner. Their closure must be checked against the final source; this report does not silently convert a recommendation into a completed correction.

### Precision and interpretation observations

- The largest price discrepancy occurred at spot/strike $10,000, ten years, 20% volatility, −10% continuous rate and zero yield. It is $0.00247078/share, approximately $0.247078 per 100-share contract. The normal CDF is an approximation, and displayed cent rounding should not be presented as an exact external market reference.
- In the 432-case derivative sweep, maximum absolute delta difference was 0.00134294 and gamma difference 0.02075463. Both arose in one-day/1% volatility inputs; fixed-step finite differences can be sensitive around narrow payoff transitions. Maximum vega difference was 0.0000134944 per share per IV point, and one-day time-change difference 0.0000138028/share. These observations support the existing local-approximation caveats; no exact-Greek claim is warranted.
- Collateral reservations remain a separate liquidity constraint. They are not deducted again as a trading loss in the stress model. The supplied gross cash obligation must be interpreted separately from the marked P&L to avoid double counting.
- Long option marks in the assignment ledger are supplied accounting inputs. The ledger correctly computes equity from those inputs but does not independently establish that every user-entered mark is economically coherent or executable.
- All 26 original case briefs explicitly label fictional teaching data. Each package has at least one source link. This audit sampled primary-source support for specific contract concepts; it did not exhaustively verify every external link or every inherited teaching paragraph.

### Primary-source checks

- Assignment on one spread leg does not automatically exercise the other leg, and remaining positions/funding require action: [OIC, What happens if one leg is assigned?](https://www.optionseducation.org/getcontentasset/86b32e5f-c816-4a0c-968f-5b9a36b6363f/dfc3d011-8f63-43f6-9ed8-4b444333a1d0/understandingassignment_1.pdf).
- A collar combines long stock and put protection with a short call and a cap on upside: [OIC, Collar](https://prd-web.optionseducation.org/strategies/all-strategies/collar-protective-collar).
- Corporate actions can change contract deliverable and multiplier; no universal adjusted-share-count assumption is justified: [OIC, Options Glossary](https://prd-web.optionseducation.org/referencelibrary/optionsglossary).
- Extrinsic/time value is the premium beyond intrinsic value before expiration; time value is zero at expiration: [OIC, Options Pricing](https://prd-web.optionseducation.org/optionsoverview/options-pricing), [CME, Calculating Options Moneyness and Intrinsic Value](https://www.cmegroup.com/education/courses/introduction-to-options/calculating-options-moneyness-and-intrinsic-value).

The source descriptions above are paraphrases. They support the named concepts, not endorsement of this course.

### What this audit cannot establish

The calculations use stipulated fictional prices, model assumptions and episode fills. They do not validate broker-specific margin, assignment deadlines, historical execution, suitability, strategy profitability or future returns. Correct calculations and software tests cannot establish that a learner understands the ideas, that a human reviewer accepts the curriculum, or that the teaching improves retention. Genuine learners, elapsed follow-up time and actual knowledgeable reviewers remain necessary for those claims.

### Correction verification — November 14, 2026

The implementation owner corrected the two assessment prompts. Independent source inspection and generated-question checks now confirm:

- **QV-01 closed:** Module 1's account-return prompt says “changes from,” including the declining-balance sequence.
- **QV-02 closed:** Module 3's extrinsic-value question explicitly describes a separate before-expiration snapshot. Its arithmetic key is unchanged.
- **QV-03 partially closed:** The vega finite difference now bounds its volatility endpoints to the supported 0–5 range and divides by the actual endpoint difference. The maximum-volatility fixture produces finite price, delta, gamma, vega and time change, and the new regression passes. The distinct maximum-spot issue remains: a base spot of 10,000,000 still produces an out-of-domain upward spot bump. This is outside the current lab UI limit of 10,000, so it remains a low-priority helper-domain limitation rather than an active learner-facing failure.

Re-ran all eight focused graduate-practice/model tests successfully. Re-ran the independent audit script: all 3,724 numerical assertions still pass, including the 98 original-case relationships. The report's source/history and the residual precision limits above remain applicable. These corrections do not create human expert sign-off or learner-validation results.


### Final boundary correction verification — November 14, 2026

**QV-03 closed for both reported endpoints.** The sensitivity helper now uses a bounded vega difference at volatility 5 and a second-order backward delta difference with a backward gamma difference when an upward stock bump would exceed spot 10,000,000. Direct execution at that maximum spot produces finite price, delta, gamma, vega and one-day change; the new maximum-spot regression also passes. The reported boundary exception is resolved. Finite-difference precision limitations remain as quantified above.

All eight focused practice/model tests pass after the final correction. The portable reproduction script was rerun successfully: all 3,724 numerical assertions still pass, including the 98 case relationships. QV-01, QV-02 and QV-03 are now closed against the inspected source. The earlier entries remain as the finding and remediation history.

## Learner-validation and review workflow audit

Reviewed November 14, 2026. This is an AI-assisted technical review of the source and evidence workflow. It is not a human expert curriculum endorsement, a credential check, or a learner outcome study. No learner responses, reviewer sign-offs or retention gains were created.

### Scope and method

Read the pilot engine, teaching mutation schemas, tutor/practice/feedback/review/pilot routes, current-event query, streamed evidence export and Teaching Studio review/pilot interface. Compared the implemented rubric and stored observations against `GRADUATE_TEACHING_STANDARD.md` and `GRADUATE_PILOT_PROTOCOL.md`. Ran an isolated read-only Node probe against the pure pilot/schema functions; it made no database or production writes.

The findings below describe the reviewed source before any subsequent remediation by the primary implementation agent. Resolution should cite the corrective change and its regression evidence.

### Findings

#### V01 — The stored pilot version does not freeze the question implementation

**Priority: high for longitudinal validity.** `course-app/app/api/teaching/pilot/route.ts:27` records `TEACHING_VERSION` in enrollment, but `course-app/lib/learning-pilot.ts:19` derives later forms only from seed/stage, and lines 24 and 30–32 call the current practice generator and grader. The stored version is not checked.

The read-only probe supplied `version: 'unsupported-future-question-version'` and still received nine day-7 questions. A future generator or key change could therefore alter a frozen study between baseline and follow-up while the record still displays its original version.

**Required correction:** preserve a versioned question blueprint/key implementation, snapshot the forms with proper answer-key access control, or reject unsupported versions explicitly. Retain the original version and actual observation times. Add a regression showing that unsupported versions cannot silently produce current forms.

#### V02 — The written-review rubric has conflicting score anchors

**Priority: medium.** `GRADUATE_TEACHING_STANDARD.md:30` defines a three-point scale from 0 through 2. The review mutation schema (`course-app/lib/teaching-validation.ts:17`) and packet (`course-app/app/api/teaching/review/route.ts:12`) use 0 through 3. The UI also describes score 2 as “supported with an unresolved gap,” whereas the packet describes it as “supported, with stated limitations.”

Those are not equivalent calibration standards. Two reviewers could assign different numbers to the same quality of work before any substantive disagreement.

**Required correction:** select one anchored scale for this advanced written-review workflow and apply it consistently in the teaching standard, review packet, interface and calibration kit. Keep older, separate foundation rubrics explicitly labeled rather than silently converting past scores.

#### V03 — The current-event projection hides previous independent ratings

**Priority: medium.** The review route appends every review of a given submission under the same entity ID (`course-app/app/api/teaching/review/route.ts:28–30`). The normal teaching read selects only the greatest revision for each kind/entity (`course-app/app/api/teaching/route.ts:10–12`). The review-history interface receives that projection (`course-app/components/teaching-studio.tsx:117`).

A second reviewer’s rating therefore hides the earlier rating in normal UI history and competency attribution, although the complete export preserves both. This impedes the protocol’s requirement to preserve and compare two independent initial scores.

**Required correction:** return all bounded review records or give independent reviews distinct entities, while continuing to use current snapshots for cumulative tutor/pilot state. Preserve reviewer source labels and any subsequent reconciliation separately.

#### V04 — The built-in numerical pilot omits interpretation metadata required by the protocol

**Priority: medium for interpretation; not evidence of fabricated results.** The protocol asks for prior experience, confidence and assistance (`GRADUATE_PILOT_PROTOCOL.md:13–15,20,29`). The stored pilot result and submit schema contain answers, score, minutes and clarity, but no confidence, assistance or prior-exposure observations (`course-app/lib/learning-pilot.ts:34`, `course-app/lib/teaching-validation.ts:22`). The read-only schema probe confirmed that additional `confidence`/`assistance` fields are currently rejected by strict validation.

Consequently, a tutor-assisted response and an unassisted response can receive the same numerical result without their difference appearing in the pilot result. Prior use of the course can also precede an apparently new baseline. The interface properly warns that these observations are not a controlled estimate, but cannot reconstruct the missing information later.

**Recommended correction:** capture clearly labeled self-reported confidence and assistance, and preserve actual prior course-use evidence at enrollment where available. Do not fill absent historical fields with “none.” Keep full written-case assessment and independent ratings distinct from arithmetic practice.

### Controls confirmed

- Pilot forms are gated by server time, not a client-supplied completion timestamp. The probe confirmed day 7 is scheduled one second before the boundary, available at the boundary and missed at day 14.
- The baseline must exist before delayed forms become available. Completed stages cannot be resubmitted through the pure engine.
- Pilot module selection is fixed at enrollment. The strict schema requires three distinct module IDs.
- The numeric answer set must match all issued question IDs exactly; non-finite answers and incomplete sets are rejected.
- Teaching mutations authenticate and scope reads/writes to the current user. Revision checks plus a unique owner/kind/entity/revision index protect racing writes.
- Review evidence must be an exact quotation of saved learner writing, and criterion names must match the saved submission’s original rubric.
- Reviewer identity is explicitly reported rather than verified. The interface distinguishes self-review from external feedback reported by the learner.
- Automated feedback refuses to reinterpret a historical submission against a changed current teaching packet (`course-app/app/api/teaching/feedback/route.ts:13`).
- Active tutor questions omit expected answers. Help, corrections and transfer attempts remain explicit in the saved session.
- Normal tutoring reads use current snapshots, and full history exports are streamed in bounded batches. This avoids the earlier quadratic cumulative-history loading pattern.

### Limits and acceptance evidence still needed

No actual participant pilot, independent human rating or external expert approval was observed or performed in this review. The software can preserve those activities, but source inspection cannot manufacture them. A complete validation claim needs dated learner work, assistance/exposure records, actual 7-/30-day observations or explicit missingness, qualified independent reviewers, both initial ratings, a discrepancy record and a defensible interpretation.

The built-in forms use known numerical question families; correctly withholding a key does not automatically make a form a genuinely unfamiliar written transfer assessment. Use the facilitator-controlled parallel case materials and independent rating process to assess decision reasoning. Do not use simulated P&L, completion counts or a high arithmetic average as a substitute.

### Remediation verification — November 14, 2026

The primary implementation agent corrected the four findings. A subsequent read-only source review and six focused tests confirmed these closures:

| Finding | Status | Observed correction and verification |
| --- | --- | --- |
| V01 | Closed for current automatic forms | `lib/learning-pilot.ts:6–24` now supplies `PILOT_QUESTION_VERSION`, `freezePilotBlueprint` and a deterministic signature covering all three forms' questions, expected results and explanations. `pilotQuestions` asserts the saved version/signature before administration; `completePilot` uses that same gate. Unsupported versions and changed seeds/signatures are rejected by the new regression. A started pilot cannot be refrozen. |
| V02 | Closed | `GRADUATE_TEACHING_STANDARD.md:30` now uses the same 0–3 advanced written-review scale as the API packet, mutation schema and UI. Score 2 is consistently supported work with stated limitations. Separate earlier foundation rubrics remain separate assessment systems. |
| V03 | Closed | `app/api/teaching/route.ts:12` retains all review events while still selecting only current cumulative snapshots for other kinds. The review history can therefore display both reviewers' original records. `lib/review-calibration.ts` and its UI compare distinct reported external names on the same saved submission, exclude self-review, and prevent repeated ratings by one named person from manufacturing additional independent raters. |
| V04 | Closed for new app pilot records | The enrollment schema now requires consent and a prior-experience choice. The route captures actual prior practice-set, submitted-memo and distinct tutor-session counts. New submission requests require self-reported confidence and assistance, and the result/interface/export preserve them. Optional type fields preserve honest “not recorded” handling for older evidence rather than inventing historical answers. |

Executed `node --experimental-strip-types --test tests/learning-pilot.test.mjs tests/review-calibration.test.mjs tests/teaching-validation.test.mjs`: **6 tests passed, 0 failed**. This checked pilot boundary logic, unsupported/tampered blueprint rejection, distinct-rater comparison, duplicate-name handling and mutation validation. The broader live API and browser checks belong to the primary implementation agent's release verification.

Two interpretation limits remain explicit rather than being treated as defects: the descriptive calibration table uses the **latest** recorded rating per named reviewer and does not claim to be a blinded initial-agreement estimate; all earlier ratings remain in the review history/export. The blueprint signature is an accidental-drift check rather than cryptographic proof. Numerical tolerances are now defined in the question engine's exported `GRADUATE_GRADING_CONVENTION` and included in the blueprint fingerprint, so accidental tolerance changes also trigger drift protection. Maintainers must still bump the question version when other grading logic changes.

These closures establish that the software can collect the intended evidence more faithfully. They do not establish that a qualified external expert has approved the curriculum or that learners have completed a longitudinal study. The user's decision to prepare materials and recruit participants later is compatible with an empty, accurate outcome record.

title: Discrete hedge and option P&L lab
body:
# Discrete hedge and option P&L lab

Use this fictional calculation after [Module 9](LESSONS_02_BEHAVIOR.md). It shows how an option's changing value, a stock hedge, cash, and execution costs fit into one account. Short stock is used here **only as a shadow calculation**; borrow availability, margin, interest, dividends, and real execution are excluded. This is not an entry-level live strategy. [OIC explains Greek sensitivities](https://www.optionseducation.org/advancedconcepts/understanding-options-greeks); they are local model readings, not guaranteed next prices.

## Data and first decision

Start with $6,000 cash. Buy one standard 100-share call at $5.00 per share, then model selling short **50 shares** at a $100 stock price. At this moment, the call's model delta is +0.50 per share, gamma +0.02 per $1 stock move, theta −$0.05 per day, and vega +$0.10 per one IV percentage-point change. Assume no opening fees, and treat short-sale proceeds as cash for the simplified accounting ledger. A real broker can restrict their use.

| Event | Cash | Call | Stock shares | Account equity under stated marks |
| --- | ---: | --- | ---: | ---: |
| Start | $6,000 | None | 0 | $6,000 |
| Buy call at $5 | $5,500 | +1 call worth $500 | 0 | $6,000 |
| Sell 50 shares at $100 | $10,500 | +1 call worth $500 | −50 | `$10,500 + $500 − $5,000 = $6,000` |

The long call's local stock exposure is `+0.50 × 100 = +50` share equivalents. The stock short is −50 shares, giving a near-zero **initial local delta**. It does not give zero risk.

## One day later: reconcile model and observed marks

The stock rises **$4 to $104**, IV falls **one percentage point**, and **one day** passes. The call is then marked at an invented **$7.30 per share**. Holding the initial Greeks fixed for a rough approximation:

```text
Call model change per share = delta × 4 + ½ × gamma × 4² + vega × (−1) + theta × 1
                            = 0.50 × 4 + 0.5 × 0.02 × 16 − 0.10 − 0.05
                            = $2.01
Model call mark           = $5.00 + $2.01 = $7.01
Observed call mark        = $7.30
Unexplained residual      = ($7.30 − $7.01) × 100 = +$29
```

The $4 stock move is large for a *local* Greek estimate; changing Greeks, the volatility surface, model inputs, and the invented mark can all contribute to the $29 gap. Do not label the residual as free profit.

At the observed marks **before rebalancing**, call P&L is `($7.30−$5.00)×100 = +$230`. Short-stock P&L is `−50×$4 = −$200`. Portfolio P&L is **+$30**, and equity reconciles to `$10,500 + $730 − 50×$104 = $6,030`. The initial-Greek model would have estimated call +$201 and stock −$200, or **+$1**; the $29 residual connects that estimate to the observed +$30.

Suppose the new approximate call delta is +0.58, or +58 share equivalents. Selling **8 more shares at $104** brings the short-stock count to −58. Assume this rebalance costs $2. Cash becomes `$10,500 + 8×$104 − $2 = $11,330`. The call remains worth $730 and the 58-share short is marked at `$58×$104 = $6,032`, so account equity is **$6,028**. Rebalancing changed exposure and cost $2; it did not create an immediate $832 gain from the short-sale proceeds.

## A second move and an executable exit

The next day the stock reference falls to **$100**. The call reference mark is **$4.90**. Before an exit, equity is `$11,330 + $490 − 58×$100 = $6,020`, a **$20 gain** from the start after the $2 rebalance fee. The hedge's result depended on the path and rebalancing choice.

Now assume an actual close requires buying 58 shares at the **$100.10 ask**, selling the call at its **$4.80 bid**, and paying a further **$2 total exit fee**. Cash after both fills is `$11,330 − 58×$100.10 + $480 − $2 = $6,002.20`; no positions remain. Final realized P&L under these fictional fills is **+$2.20**. This difference from the $20 reference-mark gain is the cost of crossing the stated stock and option quotes plus the exit fee.

## Fresh checks before the answer key

1. If the first stock move were **+$1** with IV unchanged and one day passing, what would the initial Greeks estimate for the call's value change per share and for the option-plus-50-share hedge before fees?
2. If the one-day $4 rise occurred but the option's *executable bid* were $7.10 instead of the $7.30 reference mark, what is the liquidation-style equity before rebalancing if the short stock can be covered at a $104.10 ask? State the assumption about fills.
3. At the +$4 snapshot, what is the approximate new share-equivalent delta, and what stock action would bring it toward zero? Why might the result differ from exactly zero one moment later?
4. Name four reasons a live account's cash, equity, or feasible trade could differ from this shadow ledger.

<details>
<summary>Answers and interpretation</summary>

1. Call estimate is `0.50×1 + ½×0.02×1² − 0.05 = +$0.46/share`, or **+$46 per contract**. A 50-share short loses **$50** on a $1 stock rise, so approximate combined P&L is **−$4** before fees. Gamma and theta still matter when first-order delta is offset.
2. Assuming fills at those specified prices and no additional fee, equity would be `$10,500 + $710 − 50×$104.10 = **$6,005**`, or **+$5** from the $6,000 start. Bid/ask and available size can change; this is a scenario, not a promised liquidation.
3. Approximate call delta is `0.50 + 0.02×4 = 0.58`, or **+58 shares** for the call, so selling about **8 more shares** offsets the current −50-share hedge locally. Gamma, IV, time, discrete shares, and trading delay can immediately change delta again.
4. Any four of stock-borrow availability or fees, margin requirements, restrictions on short-sale proceeds, dividends, financing costs, partial or failed fills, wider bid/ask, stale option marks, different model Greeks, corporate-action adjustment, and broker liquidation policy. Say which would affect funding versus P&L versus ability to maintain the hedge.

</details>

**Pass standard:** Reconcile cash plus marked option minus short-stock liability at every row; explain the $29 approximation residual; distinguish marks from executable bids/asks; and solve the fresh checks without the key. For a deeper research build, feed timestamped price paths into the pricing, ledger, and execution labs under `labs/`, while preserving the omitted real-world costs as explicit assumptions.

title: Quote and order-status practice
body:
# Quote and order-status practice

Use this synthetic replay with [Module 11](LESSONS_02_BEHAVIOR.md) and the [risk guide](RISK_AND_OPERATIONS.md). It teaches what can be concluded from a quote, an order, and a broker confirmation. All times below are **Eastern Time on one fictional trading day**; the quotes and executions were invented for teaching. A displayed bid/ask, size, or midpoint does not prove that a passive limit order filled. A simulated fill is an assumption unless the replay explicitly supplies a broker execution report. [IBKR describes limits of paper fills](https://www.ibkrguides.com/orgportal/aboutpapertradingaccount.htm); for live decisions, verify the exact broker and market state.

Assume standard 100-share premium multipliers and **$1 fee per filled contract per side**. The learner's written entry screen permits a long call only when the **ask is at most $2.20**, the **spread is at most $0.20**, and the exact contract and event calendar have been checked. A buy limit is the maximum accepted price; a sell limit is the minimum accepted price. The screen creates an eligible *decision*, not a demand to trade.

## The four replay episodes

Each episode is independent. Keep the order ID, requested quantity, confirmed quantity, remaining quantity, cash, and option position separate.

| Episode / ET | Visible quote and size | Learner action or broker message |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A 15:30:00 | $2.05 bid × 4 / $2.20 ask × 3 | Screen passes. Submit buy **1** at $2.20 limit, order A1. |
| A 15:30:05 | Quote may have changed | Broker execution: A1 **1 bought at $2.20**. |
| A 15:40:00 | $2.45 bid × 1 / $2.65 ask × 2 | Submit sell **1** at $2.45 limit, order A2. |
| A 15:40:03 | Quote may have changed | Broker execution: A2 **1 sold at $2.45**. |
| B 15:30:00 | $2.00 bid × 3 / $2.60 ask × 2 | Spread is $0.60. Record the eligible market observation and abstention; no order. |
| C 15:30:00 | $2.00 bid × 5 / $2.20 ask × 4 | Submit passive buy **1** at $1.95, order C1. |
| C 15:31:00 | $2.05 bid × 5 / $2.30 ask × 4 | No execution report. |
| C 15:32:00 | $2.10 bid × 3 / $2.35 ask × 5 | Broker reports C1 canceled, **zero filled**. |
| D 15:30:00 | $2.05 bid × 4 / $2.20 ask × 1 | Submit buy **3** at $2.20 limit, order D1. The entry screen passes, but visible ask size is only one. |
| D 15:30:02 | Quote may have changed | Broker reports **1 filled at $2.20**; **2 remain live**. |
| D 15:30:03 | Quote may have changed | Trader sends a request to cancel D1's remainder; status says **pending cancellation**. |
| D 15:30:05 | Quote may have changed | Broker reports **one more filled at $2.20**, now **2 filled total**. |
| D 15:30:07 | Quote may have changed | Broker confirms remaining **1 canceled**. |

### Questions to answer before the key

1. In A, what are the confirmed gross and net P&L? What would an all-midpoint estimate show using the two displayed quotes, and why is it a different result?
2. In B, calculate the spread in dollars per contract and explain the recorded decision.
3. In C, could the two later bids establish that the $1.95 buy order filled? What is the final position, and which message establishes it?
4. In D, show position and premium-plus-fee cash outlay immediately after 15:30:02, after 15:30:05, and after 15:30:07. What was the largest remaining *possible* quantity during pending cancellation?
5. Across attempted **entry** orders A1, C1, and D1, how many contracts were requested and how many were confirmed filled? What is the completion fraction for this tiny replay? Why is it not a real fill-rate estimate for a strategy?
6. A platform freezes while D1 shows “pending cancellation.” The trader cannot tell whether the last contract filled. Write the first five facts to establish before submitting any replacement order. What must be reconciled when access returns?
7. A backtest credits every B observation as a midpoint fill, and every C order as filled after the market rose. Which two distinct errors does it make?

<details>
<summary>Replay answer key — open after recording your answers</summary>

1. A paid `$2.20 × 100 = $220` and sold for `$2.45 × 100 = $245`, so gross P&L is **+$25** and net after two $1 fees is **+$23**. Displayed entry midpoint is `(2.05+2.20)/2 = 2.125`; exit midpoint is `(2.45+2.65)/2 = 2.55`. The all-midpoint calculation is `(2.55−2.125)×100−$2 = **+$40.50**`. It is a hypothetical pricing convention; the supplied broker reports establish the +$23 result.
2. B's spread is `$2.60−$2.00 = $0.60/share`, or **$60 per contract**. It breaches both the $2.20 ask screen and $0.20 spread screen, so record **abstain**, with the quote and reason. There is no trade P&L.
3. No. The later quotes provide no execution report and do not make a passive **buy** at $1.95 marketable. The broker's cancellation message says **zero filled**. Final option position and premium cost are both zero.
4. At 15:30:02, there is **+1 contract**, premium plus fee paid **$221**, and two contracts may still fill. At 15:30:05, there are **+2**, paid **$442**, and one may still fill. At 15:30:07, **+2** remain and the final one is confirmed canceled. The largest possible D1 position during the first pending-cancel interval was **+3 contracts**. The request itself reduced no confirmed exposure.
5. Entry requests total `1+1+3 = **5 contracts**`; confirmed fills total `1+0+2 = **3**`, or **3/5 = 60%** of requested contracts. These few invented orders were selected for teaching and say nothing about live queue priority or a strategy's expected fill rate.
6. Establish the **account identity**, **actual position inventory**, **every relevant order ID**, **confirmed fill quantities/prices**, and **live/pending/canceled order statuses** from an independent broker channel or support process. Do not treat a submitted cancellation or disconnected screen as confirmation. Once access returns, reconcile broker executions, account positions, cash, fees, and the written journal before resuming. Any liquidation or hedge depends on actual status and the risk policy.
7. It assumes a fill in **B despite a written rejection rule** and invents a **C fill from subsequent price movement** even though the broker confirmed zero fills. It would both ignore abstentions and select opportunities using later information.

</details>

## Platform-outage drill: order status is unknown

This episode is separate from D. Cash starts at **$1,000** with no position. At 15:10:00 ET, a buy limit for **two** standard options at **$1.00** is submitted as E1. The app disconnects before showing any acknowledgement. At 15:11:00, an approved independent broker channel confirms E1 was accepted, **one contract filled at $1.00**, and **one remains live**. The learner asks through that channel to cancel the remainder. At 15:11:05, the broker reports the second contract filled before cancellation took effect. Assume a **$1 fee per filled contract**.

Stop and write the position and cash at 15:10:00 (unknown, so give possible states), 15:11:00, and 15:11:05. Explain why submitting E2 for another two contracts at 15:10:30 could create duplicate exposure. Then write your own broker-specific emergency contact and alternate access method *before* relying on a live account; verify that route's operating hours and what it can actually confirm. The [SEC's online-trading guidance](https://www.sec.gov/about/reports-publications/investorpubsonlinetipshtm) explicitly warns that a submitted order may have executed even when the investor did not see confirmation, and that a cancellation request must be confirmed.

<details>
<summary>Outage answer and incident runbook</summary>

At 15:10:00 the learner has **unknown actual exposure**; the possible confirmed result could range from zero to two fills until status is obtained. Do not write zero merely because the app froze. At 15:11:00 there is **+1 option** and cash is `$1,000 − $100 − $1 = **$899**`, with one order quantity still live. At 15:11:05 there are **+2 options**, cash is `$1,000 − $200 − $2 = **$798**`, and no original quantity remains unfilled. A fresh E2 for two more could allow as many as four total contracts if E1 also fully filled.

The runbook is: **(1)** stop new entry submissions; **(2)** identify account, time, exact contract, E1 order ID or broker trace, and requested quantity/limit; **(3)** use the broker's established alternate access or support channel to confirm executions, positions, and every live or pending order; **(4)** request and verify any cancellation using that broker's process, while treating exposure as unresolved until confirmed; **(5)** assess the actual position and follow the written risk and expiry plan; **(6)** after access returns, reconcile executions, cash, fees, and the journal against broker records before resuming. Preserve times and communications. Do not infer cancellation from a disconnected screen or a request acknowledgement.

</details>

## Record format for the next 30 observations

Use one row per decision, including passes and no-signal days. A separate row records every order-status change; preserve the original submitted order and any cancellation request.

```text
Timestamp and time zone; quote source and quote age:
Exact underlying, option series, multiplier, deliverable; bid/ask and sizes:
Known event and contract checks; screen result; reason to enter or abstain:
Order ID, side, quantity, limit, submission time:
Confirmed fill quantity/price/time; remaining live quantity:
Cancellation request time and confirmation time, if any:
Fees; cash and open-position change; quote-side alternative:
Known unknowns, such as queue priority or stale marks:
```

**Pass standard:** Correct all seven replay answers; reconcile every D1 status without treating pending cancellation as final; complete the 30 dated observations from Module 11; and explain why replay completion is not a live execution statistic. Rework errors on changed prices and quantities. [Module 12](LESSONS_02_BEHAVIOR.md) starts the longer decision journal required by the [eight-week risk gate](RISK_AND_OPERATIONS.md).

title: External review packet: Advanced Options Academy
body:
# External review packet: Advanced Options Academy

**Review status: awaiting an actual independent reviewer.** This is an administration packet with blank decisions. Preparing it, running software tests, or obtaining an AI-assisted technical audit does not constitute an external expert endorsement.

Course version reviewed: ____________________  
Review dates: ____________________  
Reviewer name and professional affiliation: ____________________  
Relevant derivatives, risk, research, and teaching experience: ____________________  
Evidence of those qualifications, if supplied: ____________________

## Review question and scope

Does this course provide accurate, coherent, teachable and assessable preparation for explaining options mechanics and making defensible portfolio or research decisions? Assess the specific materials inspected. “MBA-style” describes the intended teaching standard; the review does not award academic credit or accreditation.

The course contains a 64-lesson beginner route and 26 advanced teaching packages. The advanced pathway progresses from contracts and account decisions, through price behavior and execution, to quantitative methods, research and portfolio risk.
