Module 10, **The Meridian Investment Committee**, is the integrated Trade Design seminar. It requires a recommendation, a common-resource portfolio comparison, a response to changed information and a defense.

Review the [curriculum map](COURSE.md), [teaching standard](GRADUATE_TEACHING_STANDARD.md), [learner pilot protocol](GRADUATE_PILOT_PROTOCOL.md), [parallel written case forms](PILOT_PARALLEL_CASES.md), and [rating/report template](PILOT_RATING_AND_REPORT_TEMPLATE.md). The four teaching volumes and their primary references supply the substantive lessons. The app's reference library and offline course ZIP contain the teaching materials; this source checkout also contains `course-app/content/graduate.json` and the implementation.

The live app supports submitted case revisions, numerical practice, deterministic tutoring, formative text checks and attributed review records. Inspect actual submitted work before describing it as reviewed. Automated passage detection, a name entered in the review desk, or a correct numerical result is not evidence of a human's independent evaluation of the whole argument.

## Independence and review agreement

The reviewer completes these declarations; none is preselected.

- [ ] I have stated my relevant experience accurately.
- [ ] I have disclosed authorship, employment, financial, personal or other relationships that could affect this review.
- [ ] I can distinguish the materials I inspected from those I did not inspect.
- [ ] I will preserve original findings and their later resolutions rather than replace an adverse first finding.
- [ ] I will identify where my expertise ends and where another specialist is needed.

Relationships, compensation, conflicts and limits: ____________________

Permission to identify the reviewer publicly: yes / no / not yet decided. A reviewer's agreement to assess material does not grant permission to publish their name or use their institution's branding.

## Review method

1. Freeze the exact course/source version, case packet and reference dates. Record the files or app views inspected.
2. Inspect every module's objective, prerequisite, taught calculation, case, rubric and transfer prompt. Record coverage at module level; do not extrapolate a sample inspection into approval of all 26 modules.
3. Independently reconstruct the flagship's cash balances, scenario table, severe boundary and revised feasibility decisions. Check all new pilot form tables before administering them.
4. Inspect contract mechanics, lifecycle and funding in detail. Then inspect model scope, execution assumptions and research interpretation with appropriate specialists where needed.
5. Assess representative learner work using the four-dimension rubric below. Preserve quotations and calculation checks supporting each score.
6. Resolve critical findings, rerun the affected exercises, and record the reviewer’s actual final decision. Unresolved items remain visible.

Software verification evidence can inform the review, but the reviewer should inspect its coverage and limitations. A passing test is not proof that the explanation teaches well.

## Module coverage record

Use one row for each of modules 01–26, and separate rows for the beginner route, laboratories, assessment engine, feedback system and pilot protocol.

| Material/version | Inspected by/date | Objective and prerequisites | Teaching and worked example | Case and assessment | Findings or limits |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| ____________________ | ____________________ | ____________________ | ____________________ | ____________________ | ____________________ |

## Content review checklist

Mark checked only after actual inspection. A checked box means the item was examined; the findings log carries the judgment.

- [ ] Rights and obligations, premium units, deliverables and exercise cash are distinguished correctly.
- [ ] Closing, exercise, assignment, settlement and remaining positions are reconciled as separate events.
- [ ] Adjusted-contract terms are supplied explicitly; a premium multiplier is not used to infer an unspecified exercise obligation.
- [ ] Cash deadlines, collateral, marks, P&L and terminal loss are separated.
- [ ] Portfolio alternatives use the same starting resources, dates and economic objective, including retained cash and stated costs.
- [ ] Quote sides, stated fills, cancellations and unfilled orders are accounted for without invented midpoint execution.
- [ ] Model prices, local sensitivity estimates, expiration values and executable prices have distinct labels.
- [ ] Greeks, volatility and probability conventions are stated, including the limits of local approximations and model pricing weights.
- [ ] Data timestamps, missing exits, held positions, trial counts, comparator choice and dependence are treated honestly.
- [ ] Synthetic, published-series and historical-contract evidence support different, explicitly limited conclusions.
- [ ] Source references are primary, relevant, dated where needed, and do not imply affiliation or endorsement.
- [ ] Recommendations follow a stated mandate and uncertainty; profit is not used as a substitute for reasoning quality.

## Teaching and assessment checklist

- [ ] A learner can identify the decision a lesson helps answer and the prerequisite knowledge it assumes.
- [ ] Examples explain the units and reasoning, and provide meaningful misconception correction.
- [ ] Guided practice progresses toward independent work without releasing the key before the first attempt.
- [ ] Staged cases preserve what was known before the update; hindsight is not rewarded as foresight.
- [ ] Alternatives can be compared fairly, and more than one recommendation may earn credit when supported.
- [ ] Rubric descriptions distinguish incomplete evidence, correct calculation and a defended decision.
- [ ] Rubric language and score scales agree across documents, review packets and the app.
- [ ] Reviewers distinguish self-review, an external review reported by a learner, and independently verified review evidence.
- [ ] Delayed checks record actual elapsed days and assistance; seen item families are not described as unseen examinations.
- [ ] Parallel forms have checked keys and comparable intended objectives; form difficulty is investigated before interpreting score changes.
- [ ] Essential activities can be completed with keyboard navigation and readable non-chart information. Record the accessibility checks actually performed.
- [ ] A learner pilot measures unfamiliar-case reasoning and retention, and retains missing or adverse results.

## Analytic rubric for written case work

Use **0–3 per dimension**, matching the current app review desk. A missing score is blank, not zero. Record an exact quotation or a reproducible calculation as evidence. A sum out of 12 is descriptive; unresolved contract or funding errors cannot be compensated for by polished prose.

| Dimension | 0: missing or materially wrong | 1: partial or insufficiently defended | 2: supported with stated limitations | 3: reproducible, challenged and defended |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Contract, units and calculation | Material unit, obligation, position or cash result is wrong or absent. | Some working is correct, but missing steps or an unresolved error prevent reproduction. | Correct contract terms and principal cash/scenario calculations are shown, with relevant assumptions and limits. | A second reader can reproduce the complete ledger; boundary/adverse cases and changed-input checks support the result. |
| Objective and alternatives | No usable mandate or fair comparison; a strategy label substitutes for a decision. | An objective and alternative are named, but the comparison omits a material tradeoff or changes resources. | A recommendation follows the stated objective and compares a relevant alternative under common resources. | The strongest opposing alternative is fairly represented, and the conditions favoring either choice are defended. |
| Risk and evidence | Unsupported certainty, concealed assumptions, or missing funding/operational exposure changes the conclusion. | Risk categories are named without showing their consequence, or evidence scope is overstated. | Known facts, assumptions, costs, uncertainty and relevant operational limits are distinguished. | A consequential adverse scenario and invalidation condition are tested; source/evidence limits constrain the conclusion. |
| Revision and communication | The first answer is missing or the update is ignored or silently substituted. | A revision is asserted with weak causal explanation or an unclear audit trail. | Initial and revised views are preserved and the update produces an explained revision or defended continuation. | A concise defense addresses a serious challenge, reproduces its numerical effect and identifies any remaining uncertainty. |

**Critical flags:** wrong deliverable or exercise cash; unexplained missing position; invented fill; failure to meet a stated cash deadline; use of future information; unreported tried variants; an unsupported guarantee. Identify the exact flag and affected conclusion. Require remediation and a changed follow-up case. The reviewer may still score other dimensions, while leaving acceptance pending.

## Blinded paired rating and calibration

Use two knowledgeable raters for a shared calibration subset. Give each a pseudonymous answer packet with its exact case assumptions, but hide the learner's identity, stage label, earlier scores and the other rater's scores. Retain form identity where it is needed to apply the correct key. Do not hide a material contract term to create artificial blindness.

Each rater independently records four scores, critical flags, evidence quotations and one challenge. Freeze those original ratings before discussion. Reconcile any difference greater than one point in a dimension, any disagreement about a critical flag, or any disagreement about acceptance. Record both originals and an adjudicated interpretation. Do not overwrite disagreement to make agreement appear higher. Use known annotated course submissions for calibration practice; they are not independent participant outcomes.

| Packet ID/form | Dimension | Rater A original/evidence | Rater B original/evidence | Difference and reason | Adjudication and date |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| ____________________ | ____________________ | ____________________ | ____________________ | ____________________ | ____________________ |

## Findings and correction log

Severity is the reviewer’s judgment: **critical** changes safety/accounting or a permitted conclusion; **major** materially weakens learning or assessment; **minor** affects clarity or presentation. Record uncertain findings as questions requiring resolution.

| Finding ID | File/module/version and exact location | Observed issue and independent evidence | Severity | Required correction | Author response/version | Reviewer recheck/status |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| ____________________ | ____________________ | ____________________ | ____________________ | ____________________ | ____________________ | ____________________ |

## Actual reviewer decision

Complete only after the review. No approval is supplied by this packet.

- Decision: approve for a bounded learner pilot / approve with stated conditions / revise and resubmit / outside my expertise.
- Exact material and version covered: ____________________
- Unreviewed material and exclusions: ____________________
- Open critical or major findings: ____________________
- Conditions before learner use or before public quality claims: ____________________
- Evidence supporting the decision: ____________________
- Reviewer name, signature or attributable confirmation, and actual date: ____________________
- Independent second specialist or pedagogical reviewer, where required: ____________________

Use the app review desk for actual learner-submission assessments and its export for the record. Keep course-level expert review and participant outcomes separate. A review of the course does not establish that every learner has mastered it.

title: Answer key for the foundation bridge and assessments
body:
# Answer key for the foundation bridge and assessments

Use this only after writing and saving your first attempt at [the math bridge](FOUNDATION_MATH_BRIDGE.md) or [the practice bank](FOUNDATION_ASSESSMENTS.md). If an answer is wrong, identify whether the error was the contract specification, units, formula, sign, arithmetic, or interpretation. Correct it, then solve a new version with changed numbers without viewing the key. A tutor or peer should supply the new case for a safety-critical retest.

## Math-bridge diagnostic

1. `0.0025 × $12,000 = $30`.
2. `($60 − $80) / $80 = −25%`.
3. `($80 − $60) / $60 = 33⅓%`.
4. `$1.40 × 100 = $140` quoted premium.
5. `$140 + $2 = $142` total hypothetical cost.
6. `S = 105 + 3 = $108`: `$105` is strike; `$3` is premium per share; this is expiration break-even before fees.
7. `max(−3, 0) = 0` is call intrinsic value per share; `max(3, 0) = 3` is put intrinsic value per share.
8. `$100 × 0.60 − $200 × 0.40 = −$20`. An average over assumed outcomes does not predict the next result.

## Math-bridge practice

- **Units and percentages:** The three quoted premiums cost `$35`, `$275`, and `$1,200` for one standard 100-multiplier contract before fees. The account loses `$2,000 / $10,000 = 20%` from its first value, then rebounds `$1,000 / $8,000 = 12.5%` from the low. It still stands `$1,000`, or 10% of the original $10,000, below the start.
- **Algebra:** The $50 put bought for $1.20 breaks even at `$50 − $1.20 = $48.80` at expiration before fees. With total $4 fees and multiplier 100, break-even is `$50 − $1.20 − $4/100 = $48.76`. A $60 call at $2 costs `$200 + $3 = $203` per contract including the stated fee. `floor($500 / $203) = 2` whole contracts; three would cost $609.
- **Functions:** A $105 call bought for $3 with multiplier 100 and no fees has expiration P&L of `−$300, −$300, $0, +$400` at final stock prices `$90, $105, $108, $112`, respectively.
- **Probability:** `0.90 × $10 + 0.10 × (−$120) = −$3` per toy outcome on average. The probabilities are hypothetical and a short observed streak does not establish their accuracy or an after-cost edge.

## Week 1 transfer check

1. Premium paid `$1.25 × 100 = $125`. Intrinsic value `($48 − $45) × 100 = $300`. Expiration profit `$300 − $125 = $175`; break-even `$45 + $1.25 = $46.25` before fees.
2. Ask cost `$1.40 × 100 = $140`; unchanged bid proceeds `$1.10 × 100 = $110`; difference `$30` before fees. A midpoint limit order may remain unfilled.

## Payoff formulas used for the 40 cases

All formulas below use the **per-share** premium `P`, stock price at expiration `S`, strike `K`, premium multiplier `M = 100`, and total hypothetical fees `F`. Intrinsic value in the table is the holder's favorable value, and it is the writer's obligation amount in the simplified expiration accounting.

| Position | Net expiration P&L | After-fee break-even | Greatest idealized expiration loss |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Long call | `M × max(S − K, 0) − M × P − F` | `K + P + F/M` | `M × P + F` |
| Long put | `M × max(K − S, 0) − M × P − F` | `K − P − F/M` | `M × P + F` |
| Short uncovered call | `M × P − M × max(S − K, 0) − F` | `K + P − F/M` | No finite theoretical ceiling |
| Short put | `M × P − M × max(K − S, 0) − F` | `K − P + F/M` | `M × K − M × P + F`, at `S = 0` |

An in-the-money short standard call creates an obligation to deliver 100 shares and receive `100 × K` strike cash if assigned. An in-the-money short standard put creates an obligation to pay `100 × K` and receive 100 shares if assigned. The table is arithmetic at expiration; it does not predict assignment timing or the broker's account treatment.

| Case | Premium cash | Intrinsic value/obligation | Net P&L | After-fee break-even | Greatest modeled expiration loss |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 01 | −$150.00 | $0.00 | −$152.00 | $51.52 | $152.00 |
| 02 | −$250.00 | $200.00 | −$52.00 | $62.52 | $252.00 |

## Mixed safety exam answers

1. A physically settled standard stock call holder can buy the shares at the strike; an assigned call writer must deliver them. A put holder can sell the shares at the strike; an assigned put writer must buy them. Premium is compensation received, not a loss ceiling. An uncovered short call has no finite theoretical loss ceiling.
2. Ask cost `$1.45 × 100 = $145`; displayed bid proceeds `$1.25 × 100 = $125`; unchanged ask-to-bid difference `$20` before fees. The $1.70 last trade is a historical execution, not a current sale price. Displayed prices can change or have insufficient size.
3. Premium dollars `$0.20 × 100 = $20`. Delivered shares are worth `10 × $8 = $80`; after paying the specified `$50`, intrinsic value is `$30`. Net expiration profit is `$30 − $20 − $2 = $8`. The premium multiplier and exercise deliverable are separate. A naive 100-current-share payoff misstates the adjusted contract. [OIC's reverse-split example](https://www.optionseducation.org/news/splits-happen) illustrates this distinction; the exact OCC adjustment memo controls a real contract.
4. The assigned short call can leave a **short 100-share stock position** when no shares were owned, with `$52 × 100 = $5,200` strike proceeds; the long $57 call remains open unless separately acted on. The long call does not automatically close the short shares. Actual broker treatment and funding should be checked.
5. Pay `$45 × 100 = $4,500` and receive 100 shares. Relative to $1,000 free cash alone, the purchase needs `$3,500` more; other account assets and the broker's actions can affect how the account handles it.
6. Intrinsic value `($83 − $80) × 100 = $300`; premium paid `$400`; after-fee P&L `$300 − $400 − $2 = −$102`. After-fee break-even `$80 + $4 + $2/100 = $84.02` at expiration.
7. Loss `($60 − $80) / $80 = −25%`. Recovery from $60 requires `($80 − $60) / $60 = 33⅓%`.
8. Cap `$20,000 × 0.0025 = $50`. First contract costs `$0.45 × 100 + $2 = $47`, so one fits and two cost $94. Second quote costs `$0.55 × 100 + $2 = $57`, so zero fit. Choose the largest **whole-number** quantity whose total exposure stays at or below the budget; never round a fraction upward.
9. No. A short American-style option can be assigned following holder exercise; an after-hours move and exercise instructions may matter. Check exact product rules, last trading time, long-holder instruction cutoff, and the broker's procedures. A closing order must actually fill to remove the short-option exposure. [FINRA's assignment explanation](https://www.finra.org/investors/insights/trading-options-understanding-assignment) covers the risk.
10. `(2,015 − 2,000) × 100 = $1,500` cash; zero index shares arrive under the stated cash-settled contract.
11. The shares gain `(80 − 70) × 100 = $1,000`; assigned short call loses `(80 − 75) × 100 = $500` of that rise; premium received is `$200`; fees are `$2`. Combined P&L is `$1,000 − $500 + $200 − $2 = $698`. Equivalently, shares sold at $75 make `$500` over their $70 cost, plus $200 premium less $2 fees.
12. No. The premium multiplier and adjusted exercise deliverable are missing; the exercise payment and settlement terms also need checking. Confirm the exact series and applicable [OCC information memo](https://infomemo.theocc.com/infomemo/search-memo), then verify with the broker's contract display before calculation.

title: Foundation practice and independent checks
body:
# Foundation practice and independent checks

Use the Week 1 check after [the opening lesson](ADVANCED_FIRST_WEEK.md), the 40 cases after Module 3 in [Volume 1](LESSONS_01_FOUNDATIONS.md), and the mixed exam after Module 6. Complete [the practical math bridge](FOUNDATION_MATH_BRIDGE.md) if any of its diagnostic questions were difficult. These are invented classroom contracts, not orders. Record every answer and your reasoning before opening [the separate answer key](FOUNDATION_ANSWER_KEY.md). Save first attempts; a later corrected answer is evidence of learning, not an erased mistake.

## Week 1 transfer check

These two cases use different numbers from [the opening lesson](ADVANCED_FIRST_WEEK.md). Try them without notes after its ten questions. Use standard stock options with a 100-share premium multiplier and no fees.

1. Buy one $45 call for $1.25. If the stock finishes at $48, calculate the premium paid, intrinsic value, and expiration profit. What is the expiration break-even price?
2. A call displays a $1.10 bid and $1.40 ask. Calculate the displayed one-contract cost to buy, proceeds from an immediate sale at an unchanged bid, and the difference. Does a midpoint order guarantee a fill?

Find their answers in [the separate key](FOUNDATION_ANSWER_KEY.md) only after committing your attempt. These are a transfer check for Week 1; the later 40 cases are Module 3's gate.

## Forty fresh expiration-payoff cases

Every row is **one standard, physically settled stock option** with premium multiplier **100** and deliverable **100 shares**. The premium is quoted in dollars per share. `F` is a hypothetical **total dollar fee for that position**, stated separately from premium. `S` is the stock price at expiration. Assume the option's intrinsic value is realized under the classroom expiration model; real exercise instructions, assignment, and broker procedures need separate checks.

For **each** row calculate: (a) premium cash paid or received, (b) intrinsic value or obligation, (c) total expiration profit or loss **after F**, (d) expiration break-even stock price **after F**, and (e) greatest idealized expiration loss, if it has a finite ceiling. For short puts, evaluate the maximum at stock price zero; for uncovered short calls, state that the theoretical loss has no finite ceiling. State the obligation separately for each short position that finishes in the money. Do not infer the actual broker's processing from the classroom model.

**Pass standard:** At least 36 of 40 complete rows correct on first attempt, with every premium-multiplier conversion, maximum-loss classification, and share/cash obligation correct after a new attempt. If you miss any safety-critical item, work a newly generated case with different numbers before advancing. Your tutor or peer can create one by changing K, premium, S, and F while keeping the stated contract terms. Do not retake only memorized rows. The compact numeric key and formulas are in [FOUNDATION_ANSWER_KEY.md](FOUNDATION_ANSWER_KEY.md).

For a fresh, reproducible changed-number retest, run `python3 scripts/generate_foundation_cases.py --seed 20261027 --output-dir practice_retest` from the project root. It writes separate question and answer Markdown files. Change the seed for each later attempt, keep the seed and first answers in [your learning record](LEARNING_RECORD_TEMPLATE.md), and open the generated key only afterward. The generator covers the same four standard-option position types; adjusted contracts and assignment remain separate safety exams.

## Mixed safety exam: attempt without notes

The numbers and situations here differ from the teaching examples. For numerical questions, show inputs, units, formula or cash-flow table, and answer. Where an exact contract term or broker procedure is missing, say what you would check.

1. For a physically settled stock **call** and **put**, state the buyer's right and the assigned writer's obligation. Does receiving premium cap a writer's loss?
2. A standard option shows `$1.25 bid / $1.45 ask`, a past last trade of `$1.70`, and multiplier 100. What is the displayed one-contract ask cost, bid proceeds, and immediate ask-to-bid difference before fees? Is the last trade a current sale price?
3. An **adjusted call** has quoted premium `$0.20` with premium multiplier 100. Its exact contract sheet says exercise requires **$50 cash** and delivers **10 current shares**, each worth $8 at the classroom settlement point. Total hypothetical fees are $2. Compute premium dollars, exercise value, intrinsic value, and net expiration profit. Explain why multiplying `(8 − 0.50) × 100` would be wrong.
4. You are short one standard $52 call and long one standard $57 call, with no shares. The short call is assigned early. Before any further action, what stock position, strike cash flow, and option position can appear? Does the long call automatically close?
5. You are assigned on one standard $45 put. What shares and strike cash move? If the account holds only $1,000 free cash, how much additional cash would the $4,500 purchase require before considering other account assets or broker action?
6. You buy one standard $80 call for $4. The stock finishes at $83; hypothetical fees total $2. What is the after-fee expiration profit or loss, and the after-fee break-even price?
7. A stock bought at $80 falls to $60. What was the percentage loss? What percentage gain from $60 restores $80?
8. A hypothetical $20,000 practice account has a classroom new-position risk cap of 0.25%. One long option costs `$0.45 × 100` plus $2 fees. How many whole contracts fit that cap? What if the quote is $0.55 instead? Explain the rounding rule.
9. A short American-style stock call appears out of the money at the regular close. Can you conclude it cannot be assigned that evening? What timing and broker facts would you check?
10. A cash-settled index call has strike 2,000, final settlement value 2,015, and multiplier 100. What cash amount does the long holder receive under the simplified exercise calculation? How many index shares arrive?
11. A learner owns 100 shares bought at $70 and sold one standard $75 call for $2. The stock finishes at $80 and the short call is assigned. Assume a $2 total hypothetical fee. Calculate combined stock-plus-call profit relative to original share cost.
12. A chain shows an option premium of $1.50 but hides its premium multiplier and adjusted deliverable. Can you compute the one-contract premium dollars and assignment shares with confidence? Name the missing contract fields and an authoritative place to verify an adjustment.

**Pass standard:** At least 11 of 12 correct on a first attempt; items 1, 3–5, 8–10, and 12 are safety-critical and must be correct on a fresh retest if missed. Explain every share and cash amount. A tutor or peer should change the numbers and scenario order for the retest. Until the operational cases are correct, stay in observation mode. This assessment is a foundation gate, not permission for live trading.

title: Practical math bridge for options
body:
# Practical math bridge for options

Use this bridge alongside Modules 1–6 if percentages, algebra, or probability are new. The numbers are classroom examples. No coding is required. If you already know Python, use the optional code checks **after** working each example by hand; otherwise use an ordinary calculator. Continue a topic until you can explain the units and solve a new version without notes. The bridge can extend the 104-week calendar; it is not a race.

## Quick diagnostic

Write an answer and units for each question before opening [the separate answer key](FOUNDATION_ANSWER_KEY.md). A wrong answer is a topic to study, not a reason to guess about a real contract.

1. What is 0.25% of $12,000?
2. A share falls from $80 to $60. What percentage did it lose, using $80 as the starting amount?
3. What percentage gain on $60 returns it to $80?
4. An option is quoted at $1.40 per share with a 100-share premium multiplier. What is the quoted premium for one contract before fees?
5. The same contract requires a total hypothetical $2 fee. What is the buyer's total cost?
6. Solve `S − 105 − 3 = 0` for `S`. Label what each number means for a $105 call bought for $3.
7. Calculate `max(92 − 95, 0)` and `max(95 − 92, 0)`. Which is a call's intrinsic value and which is a put's at stock price $92 and strike $95?
8. A hypothetical outcome is +$100 with 60% probability and −$200 with 40% probability. What is its expected dollar result? Does that result predict the next outcome?

If questions 1–5 are difficult, begin with the first two lessons below. If question 6 is difficult, work the algebra lesson. If question 8 is difficult, use the probability lesson before Module 13. Regardless of the diagnostic, complete Modules 1–6 and their operational gates.

## 1. Units and percentages

An option premium is commonly quoted **per underlying share** for a standard stock option. If the contract's premium multiplier is 100, a quote of $1.40 represents `1.40 dollars/share × 100 shares/contract = $140/contract`. Add actual applicable fees to determine cost. Record the multiplier and exercise deliverable in separate fields; an adjusted contract can keep its premium multiplier while its deliverable changes.

A percentage describes a ratio with a chosen denominator: `percentage change = (new − old) / old × 100%`. A $20 fall from $80 is `−20 / 80 = −25%`. The return from $60 back to $80 is `20 / 60 = 33⅓%`. Label the starting amount before calculating.

**Hand practice:** (a) Convert quotes of $0.35, $2.75, and $12 into dollars for one *standard* 100-multiplier contract. (b) A hypothetical account moves $10,000 → $8,000 → $9,000. Find the initial drawdown, the rebound from the low, and the remaining difference from the initial amount. Check [the key](FOUNDATION_ANSWER_KEY.md) after trying.

## 2. Algebra through break-even

An equation says two expressions are equal. To find a long call's expiration break-even, set its before-fee profit per share to zero when it finishes above the strike: `stock price − strike − premium = 0`. Add the strike and premium to both sides: `stock price = strike + premium`. A $105 call bought for $3 therefore breaks even at $108 at expiration before fees. For a long put finishing below the strike, `strike − stock price − premium = 0`, so `stock price = strike − premium`.

Fees change the equation. If a standard one-contract $105 call costs $3 per share plus a total hypothetical $2 fee, `100 × (S − 105) − 300 − 2 = 0`, giving `S = 108.02`. The extra two cents is `$2 / 100`, **not** $2 added to the stock price. Break-even is a description of expiration payoff under stated assumptions, not a forecast.

**Hand practice:** (a) Find the expiration break-even for a $50 put bought for $1.20 with no fees. (b) Repeat with a total hypothetical $4 fee and multiplier 100. (c) A standard $60 call bought for $2 has a $3 total fee. What is the highest whole number of contracts that fits a hypothetical $500 premium-plus-fee budget? Do not round a fractional contract upward. Answers are in [the key](FOUNDATION_ANSWER_KEY.md).

## 3. Functions, signs, and graphs

`max(x, 0)` chooses the larger of `x` and zero. A long call's intrinsic value per share at expiration is `max(S − K, 0)`; a long put's is `max(K − S, 0)`. The buyer's profit is intrinsic value times the premium multiplier, less premium paid and fees. The writer receives the premium but has the opposite intrinsic obligation. These are **expiration** calculations; option prices before expiration can differ.

Draw a payoff as a table first. For a standard $105 call bought for $3, calculate profit at final stock prices $90, $105, $108, and $112. Plot stock price horizontally and profit vertically. The kink at $105 is where intrinsic value first becomes positive; the zero-profit crossing is $108.

Then check your hand results with Python:

```python
import math

def long_call_expiry_pnl(final_stock, strike, premium, multiplier=100, fees=0):
    assert all(isinstance(x, (int, float)) for x in (final_stock, strike, premium, multiplier, fees))
    assert all(math.isfinite(x) for x in (final_stock, strike, premium, multiplier, fees))
    assert final_stock >= 0 and strike > 0 and premium >= 0 and multiplier > 0 and fees >= 0
    return multiplier * max(final_stock - strike, 0) - multiplier * premium - fees

for final_stock in (90, 105, 108, 112):
    print(final_stock, long_call_expiry_pnl(final_stock, 105, 3))
```

The expected P&L outputs are `−300, −300, 0, 400` dollars. Try a new strike and premium only after you can reproduce those figures by hand. This tiny function values a standard unadjusted expiration payoff under its stated assumptions; it is not a position or broker simulator.

## 4. Probability and evidence

Expected value is a weighted average over specified outcomes: `sum(probability × outcome)`. For +$100 with probability 60% and −$200 with probability 40%, the expected result is `$100 × 0.60 − $200 × 0.40 = −$20`. A 60% winning chance can still have a negative average if the losses are larger. A probability you invented for a classroom example is an **assumption**. A model estimate is also uncertain and needs validation.

The code check is straightforward:

```python
outcomes = [(0.60, 100), (0.40, -200)]
assert abs(sum(p for p, _ in outcomes) - 1) < 1e-12
print(sum(p * dollars for p, dollars in outcomes))  # -20.0
```

**Hand practice:** (a) A toy position has a 90% chance of +$10 and a 10% chance of −$120. Calculate expected P&L. (b) Say why neither toy probability nor a small streak of wins establishes a trading edge. Check [the key](FOUNDATION_ANSWER_KEY.md). Module 13 teaches probability and statistical evidence in greater depth.

## Readiness check

Move ahead when you can calculate contract dollars, percentage loss and recovery, fee-adjusted break-even, four-position expiration P&L, and a two-outcome expected value from fresh numbers. Write the units at every step. If a multiplier, deliverable, or contract term is unknown, ask for the specification instead of assuming it. Continue to [the 40-case practice bank](FOUNDATION_ASSESSMENTS.md) after Module 3; passing that bank is a separate gate.

title: Advanced Academy implementation
body:
# Advanced Academy implementation

Delivered November 14, 2026. Open **Advanced academy** in the existing Options Academy app. The beginner course remains the entry path; advanced prerequisites guide preparation and every module can be previewed.

## Phase 1 — complete teaching packages

The advanced curriculum now has 26 app-native teaching packages. Each combines the original teaching volume with an original fictional decision case, exhibits, an initial decision, new information, debrief, weak/adequate/excellent submission examples, four rubric dimensions, defense prompts, deliverables and transfer questions. Module 10 is the flagship Trade Design seminar: it compares holding shares, reducing concentration, protective puts and a collar with equal starting resources, quote-side costs, a full scenario table, a changed cash mandate and an operational extension.

The canonical source is `course-app/content/graduate.json`. Primary sources are linked in each package. Fictional data are labeled as teaching inputs. The [teaching standard](GRADUATE_TEACHING_STANDARD.md) describes the assessment and review expectations.

## Phase 2 — learning and evidence infrastructure

The app provides classrooms, a staged case studio, numeric practice, a mistake journal, competency evidence and a capstone workspace. Initial submissions, later revisions and drafts are appended to the learner's private database records. Course packets and versions are preserved with submissions. Conflicting tab saves are rejected; the learner can compare and reconcile edits. Saved work reloads, memo drafts survive navigation within the app, and browser departure warns about unsaved work. Advanced modules have bookmark URLs.

All 26 modules have three server-graded numerical practice questions per set with deterministic variations, hints and explained feedback. The server derives keys and saves the original response. Generated question families are practice; independent assessment requires a reviewer to provide genuinely unfamiliar cases. The evidence screen separates writing awaiting review from numeric results and identifies later study checks. It does not infer mastery from reading, a text-length threshold or submitting a memo.

## Phase 3 — laboratories, extension and release checks

Four laboratories require a prediction before revealing their results: equal-budget portfolio protection, European prices and Greeks, an assigned short call's cash/share ledger, and supplied partial/nonfill execution episodes. Tables accompany the explanations. Model values, local approximations, terminal values and stipulated fills remain distinct. The advanced Markdown download and full offline ZIP contain the complete teaching packages. The ZIP includes the supporting reference files; the standalone Markdown identifies additional library references by name.

The new schema migration is additive and keeps beginner progress, notes and scores intact. New advanced records begin empty. Learner-specific exports include immutable revisions and feedback; published teaching downloads exclude learner records.

## Verification

- 58 unit/content/math/validation tests pass, including 78 independent practice answer checks, pricing reference values, parity, portfolio accounting, adaptive branches, written-feedback rules, real-date pilot windows and migration preservation.
- TypeScript and repository ESLint pass.
- 24 live advanced API checks pass: authentication, owner isolation, immutable revisions, concurrent request handling, strict request validation, hidden pre-submission keys, grading and exports.
- An additional 41 teaching API checks pass: adaptive corrections, concurrent turns, exact-submission feedback and historical-packet protection, quoted review evidence, real-date pilot gates, artifact revisions, exports and owner isolation.
- The advanced live browser journey passes: 26-module navigation, commitment, revision, reload, practice, mistake history and mobile layout. Six additional mocked browser checks cover conflict recovery, draft retention and anonymous study.
- Teaching Studio and portfolio/artifact browser workflows pass: tutor resume and conflicts, assisted transfer, feedback, attributed reviews, baseline and future checks, artifact revisions, funding stress, research critique and mobile layout.
- The existing 14-stage beginner browser regression suite passes.
- The flagship scenario table and cash update were independently recalculated. A separate pricing implementation checked 90 parameter combinations; differences remained below the cent-display tolerance.
- Desktop and mobile screenshots were inspected. This is targeted accessibility/layout verification, not a full accessibility certification.

Source freshness, local Markdown links, and the production build are checked before publication. Publication outcome is reported separately by the publishing service.

## Phase 4 — adaptive teaching and learner validation workflows

The **Teaching studio** now implements adaptive sessions, submission-specific formative feedback, a review desk and a real-date learner pilot. The tutor selects priorities from saved mistakes, prerequisite checks and later study dates. Numeric errors trigger targeted explanations, assisted correction and a changed transfer question; original responses and help remain recorded. Written feedback quotes the learner's text, identifies missing reasoning, challenges selected claims and checks explicit amounts in the flagship case. Evidence detection is labeled separately from correctness or academic grading. Historical packets cannot be silently checked against changed current assumptions.

The review desk supplies the exact original case, rubric and submitted answers. Recorded reviews require quotations from the saved work, criterion scores, a challenge and a response. Self-review and external feedback reported by the learner have different labels. Neither a reviewer identity nor credentials are verified by recording a name.

The built-in pilot freezes three module blueprints, preserves a baseline and serves changed numerical forms in the day-7 and day-30 windows. Dates come from the server. The day-7 form opens seven days after baseline and closes at day 14; day 30 opens at day 30 and closes at day 45. Missing visits stay missing. It records correct answers, actual completion dates, self-reported minutes and clarity. The [full pilot protocol](GRADUATE_PILOT_PROTOCOL.md) also calls for independently administered written cases and calibrated human ratings. Actual participant results and independent expert judgments require people to complete that work; none are fabricated.

Additional scenario labs cover a joint portfolio shock with a separate gross funding ledger and a research critique with independently varying timestamp, holdout, cost and benchmark traps. The capstone workspace now preserves typed protocol, data, model, execution, stress and defense artifacts, revisions, HTTPS source links and downloadable manifests. A source link is not treated as a verified clean rerun.

Teaching events are appended with owner-scoped revision checks. Normal learning reads retrieve current snapshots; the export streams the complete history in bounded batches. This avoids loading every repeated tutoring snapshot into the learning page.

## Validation preparation completed

The owner chose to prepare materials and bring participants later. The [readiness record](VALIDATION_READINESS.md) lists the completed external review packet, four written form blueprints, separate initial/update learner packets, instructor keys, rating/report template and technical audit closures. New pilots record consent, prior experience, prior observed exposure, confidence and assistance. Question blueprints and grading tolerances are protected against accidental drift, and all recorded reviewers remain visible for calibration. No enrollment, expert approval or participant outcome was created on the owner’s behalf.

title: Advanced course learner pilot protocol
body:
# Advanced course learner pilot protocol

**Status: protocol prepared; learner pilot not yet conducted.** No participants, reviewer approvals, learning gains or retention outcomes are invented. Technical release checks do not substitute for learner evidence.

The app's **Teaching studio → Learning pilot** implements the numerical component: a frozen three-module baseline, changed parallel numerical forms, server-enforced day-7/day-30 windows, real observed scores, consent, prior experience/exposure, self-reported confidence, assistance, minutes and clarity, missing measurements and a private export. Day 7 is available on elapsed days 7–13 and day 30 on elapsed days 30–44. This component is repeated practice on known item families. The written transfer cases, participant recruitment and independent reviewer calibration below remain activities for real people. Use the review desk and capstone artifacts to preserve their actual evidence.

## First question

Does the Trade Design teaching package help learners make and explain a coherent portfolio recommendation on a fresh case, including cash constraints and a response to new information? The study concerns learning, not investment performance.

## Participants and baseline

Recruit volunteers spanning relevant entry levels and record prior options, finance and programming experience. Record the recruited and completed counts and reasons for withdrawal where volunteered. Obtain participants' agreement to the pilot and state what records will be retained. Avoid collecting personal financial details; use supplied fictional portfolios.

Before instruction, administer an unfamiliar parallel case assessing objective interpretation, units, scenario accounting, alternatives, uncertainty and communication. Ask for confidence and assistance used. Save the first attempt before feedback. Do not use the flagship case's publicly visible debrief as an unseen baseline.

## Learning and assessment sequence

1. Complete the Trade Design package with session start/end times and interruptions recorded voluntarily.
2. Capture the initial memo, revised memo, practice attempts and assistance used.
3. Administer a fresh parallel transfer case after instruction. Keep its answer key withheld until submission.
4. Administer different parallel cases approximately 7 and 30 days later. Record actual elapsed days rather than claiming exact scheduling when a visit is late.
5. Ask learners which explanation, exhibit or interaction was confusing and which error they could now explain unaided.

A parallel form must test the same underlying skill with a material change in conditions, such as a different cash need, contract quantity, exercise assumption or objective. Changed numbers alone help arithmetic practice but may not test conceptual transfer. Review all form calculations independently before use.

## Measures and interpretation

Primary evidence is the change in independently rated fresh-case reasoning using the four-dimension teaching rubric. Report each dimension separately. Also report exact arithmetic/units accuracy, cash-ledger errors, assumption omissions, incomplete submissions, time spent, assistance and retention. Distinguish independent work from assisted or already-seen practice.

Report sample sizes, missing follow-ups and the distribution of results, not just a selected average. A small convenience pilot can identify usability and teaching problems; it does not establish broad effectiveness or isolate the cause of a change. If a larger comparison is later needed, preregister its question, assignment method, outcomes, exclusions and analysis before collecting results.

## Reviewer calibration

Have at least two knowledgeable reviewers independently score a shared subset without seeing the learner's earlier scores. Compare disagreements and preserve both initial scores. Clarify rubric language using specific examples before judging remaining work. Do not label self-scored answers as independent review. A numerical error that changes funding feasibility requires remediation even if prose is strong.

## Decisions after the pilot

Revise explanations, example order or difficulty when errors cluster around the same concept. Repair any incorrect case or calculator immediately and preserve the earlier version. Repeat the affected fresh checks after the correction. Set performance targets only after reviewing a baseline; do not retroactively select a flattering threshold.

The pilot report should identify changes made, evidence supporting them, unresolved weaknesses and the next evaluation question. Publish only aggregate findings that participants agreed to share. Course completion, engagement, paper profit and time spent are not substitutes for demonstrated learning.

## Prepared administration materials

Use [the external review packet](EXTERNAL_REVIEW_PACKET.md), [four parallel written forms](PILOT_PARALLEL_CASES.md), and [the rating/report template](PILOT_RATING_AND_REPORT_TEMPLATE.md). Teaching studio provides a learner ZIP with initial packets and updates in separate files, without instructor keys, plus a review/rating guide. The complete course ZIP supplies facilitator blueprints and instructor keys. Report prior exposure to any public form; adapt and independently recheck conditions before describing an assessment as unfamiliar. The owner has chosen participant recruitment and actual administration for a later date.

title: Advanced Options Academy: teaching and assessment standard
body:
# Advanced Options Academy: teaching and assessment standard

This standard develops the existing 26-module advanced curriculum into an MBA-style finance specialization. It describes teaching quality and evidence of learning; it does not claim accreditation, independent expert sign-off or demonstrated learning gains before those reviews take place.

The canonical teaching packages are in `course-app/content/graduate.json`. Each preserves the relevant lesson from the four teaching volumes and adds a decision bridge, an original fictional case, staged information, a reproducible debrief, submission examples and reviewer questions. Module 10, **The Meridian Investment Committee**, is the flagship integrated seminar. Its alternatives use the same starting wealth, stated quote sides, premiums, fees and cash constraints.

## The teaching cycle

1. **Orient:** explain the decision the concept helps answer; name prerequisites and an observable learning outcome.
2. **Diagnose:** record the learner's intuition before showing a solution.
3. **Teach:** build an intuitive explanation, reproduce a worked calculation and identify a common misconception.
4. **Practice:** use guided and independent exercises with explicit units, assumptions and permitted conclusions.
5. **Decide:** submit a recommendation using only the initial packet, including alternatives and missing evidence.
6. **Adapt:** reveal the update, preserve the first memo and explain a revised decision or defended continuation.
7. **Defend:** answer a skeptical reviewer's numerical, operational and interpretive challenges.
8. **Transfer:** solve an unfamiliar case later, noting assistance and any previously seen solution.

The beginner route remains an accessible entry point. The advanced reference pace of four weeks per module is a planning aid. A completed reading, a saved submission, a correct arithmetic result and an independently defended project are different evidence states.

## Case and calculation requirements

Every original case must label fictional data, identify the relevant contract and accounting assumptions, and expose missing information rather than fill it with favorable guesses. A quote, a model value, an order intention, a confirmed fill and an expiration payoff must remain distinct. Portfolio comparisons include retained cash and use a common starting-resource basis. Gross funding and maximum modeled loss are different quantities.

Before release, an author or reviewer reconstructs each new numerical case independently. The flagship case requires a complete scenario table, severe boundary, fee reconciliation and updated cash-feasibility check. A change to a contract, quote side, fee convention or mandate requires rechecking all affected outputs.

## Feedback standard

Feedback identifies the misconception, explains its consequence and assigns a corrective task. A student who calculates correctly but omits the objective, alternatives, uncertainty or operational obligations has not completed the full analysis. Annotated weak, adequate and excellent samples make that distinction visible. Samples are teaching aids; copying them is not independent evidence.

The case rubric has four dimensions: contracts/units/calculation; objective/alternatives; risk/evidence; and revision/communication. Score each **0 absent or materially wrong, 1 partial with unresolved errors, 2 supported with stated limitations, 3 independently reproducible, challenged and clearly defended**. Record specific evidence for each score. Arithmetic safety errors require correction and a fresh case; a high total does not compensate for unresolved funding or contract mistakes.

Automated practice can grade narrowly specified numerical questions. It cannot certify the quality of an open-ended investment recommendation. Self-reflection is labeled self-review, and a human reviewer must actually inspect the work before it is described as independently reviewed. The app's saved submissions and practice attempts support this distinction.

## Capstone and committee defense

The capstone preserves the original question, A/B/C evidence level, methods, inputs, versions, trial log, assumptions, calculations, exceptions, failed alternatives and revisions. A reviewer should be able to change one input and ask the learner to explain the effect. A negative or inconclusive research result can meet the standard when its conclusion follows from complete, reproducible evidence.

Synthetic tests demonstrate stipulated software/accounting behavior. Published-series work supports a methodology-aware comparison. Historical-contract conclusions need suitable point-in-time contract evidence and qualified execution assumptions. None of these labels establishes future returns.

## Release and teaching evidence

Software verification checks functionality, isolation, persistence and calculations. Learner validation checks whether the instruction improves unfamiliar-case performance and retention. These are separate claims. Follow [the learner pilot protocol](GRADUATE_PILOT_PROTOCOL.md) before describing the course as proven effective.

Teaching benchmarks: [HBS case method](https://www.hbs.edu/mba/academic-experience/the-case-method) for preparation, discussion, decisions and reflection; [MIT Finance Theory I syllabus](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/15-401-finance-theory-i-fall-2008/pages/syllabus/) for analytical finance content and graded work. These references are design benchmarks, not affiliations or endorsements.

title: Study options in small daily sessions
body:
# Study options in small daily sessions

Start with [Lesson 01](beginner/01_MARKETS.md). Study one idea at a time for **10–15 minutes**. Each lesson has teaching, a worked example and a new problem with a folded answer. Read eight lessons, then take that module's checkpoint.

## Learn one idea and use it

1. Recall the previous lesson without notes for a minute or two.
2. Read today's lesson. Write down any word you cannot explain; consult the [glossary](beginner/GLOSSARY.md) only as needed.
3. Cover the worked result and redo it. Keep dollars, shares and contracts separate.
4. Answer the fresh question before opening its solution. Record your first answer even when uncertain.
5. Compare reasoning as well as the final number. Correct the exact mistake, then explain the idea in one sentence.

Stop when the session ends. If you need another day on the same concept, take it. Use the [workbook](beginner/WORKBOOK.md) for a lightweight paper record or save notes in the app. Your existing [learning record](MY_LEARNING_RECORD.md) remains available; the course does not fill in completion claims for you.

## Use checkpoints as feedback

The written modules include five-question checkpoints with folded solutions. The app has server-graded five-question checkpoints with two alternating forms. Complete all eight lessons before taking one. In the app, **5/5** passes; the next module's completion controls then open. You can preview any lesson while working toward a pass.

Write answers before checking feedback. After a miss, revisit the relevant lesson, do a changed-number problem and try the alternate form. After both forms have been seen, they are review practice; their results no longer count as unseen evidence. For a fresh test, ask a tutor to change numbers and conditions and withhold the key. A score measures this learning task, not profitability or live readiness.

The final capstone in Lesson 63 has several cases. Do one case per session if needed. Explain the account's remaining shares, options and cash, not just a profit number.

## Review before forgetting

The app first schedules a completed lesson for review after one day. Successful recalls extend the interval to three, seven, fourteen and then thirty days; a missed recall brings it back after one day. These intervals are course design choices. Reveal the answer only after trying to explain the idea without notes.

Use [the 84-session plan](beginner/REVIEW_PLAN.md) if you prefer a written schedule. At five sessions a week it is about seventeen weeks before repeats and extra capstone time. The number is a planning aid, not a promise of mastery by a date. Review queues can take priority over a new lesson.

## Ask for teaching in chat

Say **“Teach me Lesson 12 in five minutes. Explain one idea, show one example, ask a new question, and wait.”** After answering, ask for feedback on your reasoning. For a checkpoint, say **“Give me a fresh Module 3 quiz without showing the answers.”** Record any attempt you want to keep in your notes or workbook.

## Keep practice honest

Study fictional examples first. When later observing a real quote, record its source, time and delay. Paper decisions can be logged in a notebook; no broker account or deposit is needed. Keep rejected ideas and unfilled orders. Simulated fills and the [synthetic Python labs](labs/README.md) can teach a process but cannot establish executable market performance.

Once the beginner course is complete, select an [optional advanced path](MASTERY_TRACKS.md) only if it serves your goal. The original [advanced study guide](ADVANCED_STUDY_GUIDE.md) describes the longer research program. The beginner course does not require calculus or Python.

## Advanced case seminars in the app

Open **Advanced academy** for the 26-module teaching pathway. Begin with the prerequisite guidance for the selected module; Module 10 provides a complete Trade Design case seminar. Read its teaching sections, examine the exhibits, and save a first recommendation with calculations and risks before opening the new information. Save a revised submission after the update, then compare your reasoning with the rubric, annotated examples, and debrief. A defensible choice can differ from the model submission if its assumptions and calculations support it.

Use numeric practice to locate a specific misconception. Keep the first answer and feedback in your evidence history, revisit its teaching section, and solve a changed case. Come back at least seven days later for a retention check. The app distinguishes numeric practice from written work awaiting review. Bring major submissions and the capstone to a knowledgeable reviewer, using the defense prompts to challenge the reasoning.

Save drafts before leaving the academy. The advanced evidence export preserves submissions, revisions, numeric feedback, and the version of the teaching packet used. For offline study, download the advanced Markdown course from the academy; it is also included in the full course ZIP.

title: Learning record template
body:
# Learning record template

Make a personal copy of this file, date it, and preserve earlier entries. The [course map](COURSE.md) provides the module gates; this record stores evidence behind a pass decision. A checkmark without the original answer, corrected reasoning, and later retest is incomplete. The intervals below are a study aid, not a measured prediction of retention.

## Starting diagnostic

```text
Date and time zone:
Hours per week available:
Goal path(s) from MASTERY_TRACKS.md:
Options experience and contract knowledge:
Math diagnostic from FOUNDATION_MATH_BRIDGE.md: first-attempt score and errors:
Python challenge: read CSV, validate numeric/date values, calculate a hand-checked return, and rerun from a clean directory:
Source files or notes for the challenge:
Starting module and reason:
Prerequisites to practice alongside it:
```

Passing the Python challenge lets an experienced programmer replace introductory syntax work in Module 15 with an advanced reproducibility or testing task. The Module 15 artifact and Gate C still apply. Options mechanics, mathematics, and safety scenarios must each be demonstrated independently.

## One record for each assessment attempt

```text
Date/time and module:
Assessment identifier and version (keep the prompt):
Conditions: closed notes / open notes / time allowed:
My original answer, calculation, and confidence before checking:
First-attempt score and required standard:
Error category: units / contract / arithmetic / model / data / execution / operations / explanation:
Exact incorrect step and corrected reasoning:
Source or contract specification used to resolve uncertainty:
Artifact or code path, data version, and result hash if relevant:
Remediation exercise and result:
Fresh retest identifier and date:
Gate decision, evidence link, and reviewer:
```

For safety-critical errors, solve a *fresh* case after correcting the reasoning. Recheck important ideas after a day, about a week, and about a month, adjusting the intervals to actual results. Keep the first answer as well as the correction so progress is visible.

## Weekly study and decision record

```text
Week, module, dates, and actual study hours:
Concepts explained from memory:
Problems completed; first-attempt and retest results:
One calculation checked by hand and, if useful, by Python:
Market observation: source, time zone, timestamp, bid/ask, exact contract:
Errors or near misses, their cause, and the next fresh case:
Current module artifact and reproducible file path:
Paper decisions, no-trade decisions, and failed orders, if permitted at this stage:
One forecast or expectation stated before an outcome, if studying research:
What changed my mind this week:
Next week's single main focus:
```

Observations from delayed quotes are suitable for practice but are not proof of an available live fill. When paper simulation begins, maintain the eight-week decision record and requirements in [the risk guide](RISK_AND_OPERATIONS.md) even if it spans more than one course module.

## Project evidence index

| Date | Module or path | Hypothesis or skill | First attempt | Retest | Artifact/version | Reviewer and decision |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  |  |  |  |  |  |  |

Keep failed ideas, rejected orders, empty days, and revised reports. They are part of the evidence needed to audit a process.

## A common review rubric

Score each dimension **0 = absent or wrong**, **1 = partly correct with an unexplained gap**, or **2 = independently reproducible and explained**. Save the reviewer's specific counterexample and the learner's response. A total score is useful for feedback; the module's stated gate still controls advancement.

| Dimension | What earns 2 |
| --- | --- |
| Contract and units | Exact series, premium multiplier, exercise deliverable, dates, dollars, shares, and assumptions are correct. |
| Calculation or code | A hand check and a clean rerun agree; boundary or adverse cases have been tried. |
| Decision and operations | Cash, shares, remaining options, order status, nonfills, fees, and funding are reconciled when relevant. |
| Evidence and interpretation | Source, timestamp, benchmark, failed alternatives, uncertainty, and permitted conclusion match the project. |

For Modules 1–12, any error about contract size, maximum loss, exercise, assignment, settlement, or funding requires a fresh correct case even if the total score is high. For Modules 13–26, a code pass with wrong timestamps, unsupported fills, or concealed variants fails the research gate. An independent reviewer should change one input or assumption and ask for a new explanation before signing off on a major gate.

title: Lessons 1–6: the beginner foundation
body:
# Lessons 1–6: the beginner foundation

This is the first **24 weeks** of the course, written as lessons rather than a list of topics. Read Module 1's lesson below, then complete its [Week 1 practice](ADVANCED_FIRST_WEEK.md) and return to the chapter plan. If percentages or algebra are new, use the [practical math bridge](FOUNDATION_MATH_BRIDGE.md) from the beginning; if you already know Python, use its code checks while still solving by hand. The [foundation assessment bank](FOUNDATION_ASSESSMENTS.md) supplies fresh cases and a separate answer key. Continue these chapters in order. All prices and contracts below are invented classroom examples. Unless a section says otherwise, examples use a **standard, physically settled stock option for 100 shares**, ignore fees until explicitly added, and value positions **at expiration**. Actual contract terms and a broker's procedures must be checked before any real order. The [SEC's stock-options bulletin](https://www.investor.gov/introduction-investing/general-resources/news-alerts/alerts-bulletins/investor-bulletins-63) and the [OCC disclosure document](https://www.theocc.com/company-information/documents-and-archives/options-disclosure-document) are the primary references.

Each of the four weeks in a chapter uses the same 10-hour budget: **2 hours lesson/source reading, 3 hours worked practice, 2 hours observation without orders, 2 hours notes or a small project, and 1 hour recall and error correction**. The table in each chapter tells you what to do with those hours. Write answers before opening the key. Rework misses without looking, then explain the idea aloud in ordinary language.

## Module 1 (weeks 1–4): money, markets, and the purpose of trading

### Lesson

Start with an everyday distinction. **Saving** puts money aside for a future need. **Investing** puts money into assets whose value and cash flows are uncertain, often for years. **Trading** means making shorter-horizon decisions to buy, sell, or hedge. None of these words describes a guaranteed return. An options position can change value much faster than a stock position, so the first trading skill is knowing which money is available for risk and which money pays for ordinary life. In your notebook, keep living expenses, emergency reserves, debt obligations, and potential trading capital as separate lines. A classroom exercise can use hypothetical capital even if you have no money available for trading.

A **share of stock** is a unit of ownership in a company. An **exchange-traded fund (ETF)** is a fund whose shares trade on an exchange and hold assets according to its rules. An **index** is a calculated measure, such as a basket's level; the index itself is not a share you can take home. Options can reference a stock, ETF, or index, but their contract terms may differ. Before learning an option, learn to ask what its underlying actually is. The [SEC's investing basics](https://www.investor.gov/introduction-investing/investing-basics/investment-products) is a starting reference for products. We will use an imaginary company, ABC, rather than a real ticker so that examples cannot be mistaken for recommendations.

Trading needs infrastructure. A **broker** is the firm through which a customer submits orders and maintains an account. An **exchange** organizes trading and publishes market rules and prices. The **Options Clearing Corporation (OCC)** clears standardized U.S. listed securities options and sets out the rights, obligations, exercise, and assignment framework in its [disclosure document](https://www.theocc.com/company-information/documents-and-archives/options-disclosure-document). The broker determines what option strategies an account is approved to use; [the SEC says approval levels and allowed strategies vary by firm](https://www.investor.gov/introduction-investing/general-resources/news-alerts/alerts-bulletins/investor-bulletins-77). You do not need an options account to complete the first part of this course.

Measure outcomes in both dollars and percentages. If 100 ABC shares cost $50 each, the position costs $5,000. At $55 each, its market value is $5,500 and its gain is $500, or `500 / 5,000 = 10%` before costs and taxes. At $45, the loss is $500, or 10%. A loss and its recovery are asymmetric: $5,000 falling by 50% becomes $2,500. A later 50% rise produces $3,750, still below the start. To return to $5,000 from $2,500 requires a 100% gain. This is why avoiding a severe loss matters more than collecting impressive small wins.

Time and alternatives matter as much as the percentage. A 10% gain over one year and a 10% gain over ten years describe different outcomes. A $500 profit from risking nearly all of a small account is different from the same profit on a well-controlled exposure. A trading journal should therefore record the starting amount, dates, capital tied up, worst loss along the way, and a sensible comparison such as holding the underlying or staying in cash. This does not mean cash is always better; it means you should be able to describe what extra risk an option is supposed to solve. The eventual aim is a repeatable decision process, not a striking single result.

**Vocabulary to own:** asset, stock, ETF, index, broker, exchange, clearinghouse, cost basis, return, drawdown, liquidity, risk capital. A *drawdown* is a decline from a prior peak; it is not automatically the same as the total loss on one trade. Do not use a high percentage return to judge skill until you know the starting capital, risk taken, fees, and the time period.

**Common mistakes to catch:** calling an index a share, treating all account cash as available for a loss, or comparing two percentages without their time periods and drawdowns.

### Four teaching weeks

| Week | Use the 2/3/2/2/1-hour pattern |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | Complete [ADVANCED_FIRST_WEEK.md](ADVANCED_FIRST_WEEK.md); rewrite its seven key definitions in your own words; observe one stock and one ETF quote without placing an order; correct the quiz. |
| 2 | Read the SEC product overview. Make a one-page map of stock, ETF, index, broker, exchange, and OCC; calculate ten stock-position dollar values and returns. Use the [math bridge](FOUNDATION_MATH_BRIDGE.md) for percentages and units as needed. |
| 3 | Write a hypothetical budget separating essential money from an imaginary practice account; observe how a stock and ETF price move over five sessions; note that an index is a calculation, not a deliverable share. |
| 4 | Work drawdown and recovery problems, teach the broker/exchange/OCC map aloud, and take the closed-note check below. Correct the math-bridge diagnostic if needed. |

### Try it before opening the answers

1. You buy 20 ABC shares at $40. What was the cost, and what is the percentage return if the share price becomes $44, before costs?
2. An account moves from $8,000 to $6,000. What is its drawdown from that peak? What return on $6,000 is needed to reach $8,000 again?
3. Which is a calculated level rather than a share: ABC stock, ABC ETF, or ABC index?
4. Name the distinct jobs of broker, exchange, and OCC in one sentence each.
5. Why is a 40% gain by itself insufficient evidence that someone is a skilled trader?

<details><summary>Module 1 worked answers</summary>

1. Cost is `20 × $40 = $800`. New value is `20 × $44 = $880`. Gain is `$80 / $800 = 10%`.
2. Loss is `$2,000 / $8,000 = 25%`. Recovery requires `$2,000 / $6,000 = 33⅓%`, not 25%.
3. The index. A stock or ETF has tradable shares; an index is a calculated reference level.
4. Broker handles the customer account and order; exchange runs the trading venue and rules; OCC clears listed option contracts and their exercise/assignment obligations.
5. You need the time period, starting capital, losses and drawdowns, position size, fees, and a fair benchmark; one gain could follow a large gamble.

</details>

**Pass gate:** 5/5 with correct arithmetic and a plain-language explanation. Produce a one-page map of the market and a hypothetical budget; no real order is part of this gate.

## Module 2 (weeks 5–8): how to read an option quote

### Lesson

A quote is an invitation to trade at indicated prices, not a record of what you will earn. The **bid** is the displayed price at which someone is currently willing to buy; the **ask** or offer is the displayed price at which someone is willing to sell. The **bid–ask spread** is the difference. If a standard 100-share stock option has a bid of $2.10 and an ask of $2.30, buying one at the displayed ask costs `$2.30 × 100 = $230`. If the market is unchanged and you immediately sell at the displayed bid, you receive `$2.10 × 100 = $210`. The $20 difference is a cost before commissions. The $2.20 **midpoint** is just `(bid + ask) / 2`; nobody has promised a fill there. Quotes can move or disappear before an order arrives.

An option quote must identify more than a ticker. Record the **underlying**, **call or put**, **strike**, **expiration**, **premium multiplier**, and **exercise deliverable** as separate fields. The premium multiplier converts a per-share quote into contract dollars; the deliverable describes what exercise transfers. They can differ on adjusted contracts. The **last trade** is a past transaction, possibly at an old price. **Volume** counts contracts traded during the session. **Open interest** counts outstanding contracts under the reporting convention and may not reflect today's trades yet. Neither volume nor open interest alone guarantees that you can enter or leave at a good price. A liquid contract often has a narrower spread and accessible size, but liquidity can change when a stock moves or news breaks. [OIC's options tools](https://www.optionseducation.org/options-quotes-calculators) show delayed quotes and calculators; delayed data are for learning, not a live execution assumption.

Consider a displayed quote: `ABC Dec 18 $50 call, bid $1.45, ask $1.65, last $1.80, volume 200, open interest 4,000`. Read it from left to right. ABC is the underlying, December 18 is the expiration, $50 is the strike, and this is a call. If the deliverable is standard 100 shares, the ask represents $165 per contract. The last price of $1.80 does **not** mean the current option can be sold for $180. At the displayed bid, one contract would bring in $145 before fees. The displayed spread is $0.20 per share, or $20 per contract. Check the quote timestamp, particularly when using free delayed data.

A **market order** asks to trade promptly against available interest and can fill at prices worse than the screen last showed. A **limit order** specifies your worst acceptable price for a buy or sale, but may never fill. Imagine a buy limit at $1.55 when the ask is $1.65. The order might be filled if someone sells at $1.55; it might also sit unfilled. The $10 improvement from ask to limit is not a saving until a fill actually occurs. In later research you will count rejected and unfilled orders as part of the process, rather than inventing midpoint trades.

The same $0.20 per-share spread has different importance for different option prices. On a $10 option it is a small fraction of the premium; on a $0.30 option it consumes most of the quoted price. Calculate both the **dollar spread** and its size relative to the ask. An option may display one contract at the best bid and many at other prices, so a larger order may not all fill at the best quote. Nor does a tight screen guarantee the same liquidity during a sudden move. As a beginner, read the chain to learn how markets work, not to identify the option with the biggest percentage movement.

**Vocabulary to own:** bid, ask, midpoint, spread, last, volume, open interest, multiplier, deliverable, market order, limit order, timestamp. Read a quote as a bundle of exact contract terms plus a time-specific market, not as a single option price.

**Common mistakes to catch:** multiplying a premium quote by 100 before checking the actual premium multiplier; assuming the share deliverable must equal that multiplier; treating a last trade as today's bid; assuming a limit order must fill; or mistaking open interest for the number of contracts traded today.

### Four teaching weeks

| Week | Use the 2/3/2/2/1-hour pattern |
| --- | --- |
| 5 | Label every field in ten invented quotes; practice converting quoted per-share premiums into contract dollars; observe OIC's delayed chain. |
| 6 | Record five real delayed quotes with timestamps; compute each spread in dollars and as a fraction of the ask; watch how the quote changes without trading. |
| 7 | Compare last, bid, ask, volume, and open interest for ten contract rows. Draft ten hypothetical limit orders and state whether the screen guarantees a fill. |
| 8 | Build a 20-row quote notebook, including the underlying and contract identifiers. Audit every multiplier, timestamp, and round-trip spread calculation. |

### Try it before opening the answers

1. A standard contract is quoted $0.80 bid / $1.00 ask. What is the displayed spread per share and per contract? What is the immediate ask-to-bid loss before fees?
2. A call's last price is $2.40, but its current bid is $1.70 and ask is $1.90. At the displayed prices, how much would a one-contract marketable sale bring in before fees?
3. What contract identifiers and separate multiplier and deliverable fields should you write down before converting a quoted premium into dollars?
4. A buy limit is $1.50 while the displayed ask is $1.60. Does the limit order guarantee a $1.50 fill? What is the most it authorizes you to pay per share if it fills?
5. A contract shows high open interest but a very wide spread. What can you conclude about the price at which you will exit tomorrow?

<details><summary>Module 2 worked answers</summary>

1. Spread is `$1.00 − $0.80 = $0.20` per share, or `$20` for 100 shares. An unchanged immediate buy at ask and sell at bid loses $20 before fees.
2. `$1.70 × 100 = $170`. The $2.40 last trade does not set the current sale price. This assumes the displayed bid remains and has enough size when the order reaches it.
3. Underlying, call/put type, strike, expiration, actual **premium multiplier**, and actual **exercise deliverable** in separate fields; also record timestamp and exercise/settlement terms before acting.
4. No. It may not fill. If it fills as a standard buy limit order, it authorizes at most $1.50 per share, excluding fees.
5. You cannot know tomorrow's exit price or spread from today's open interest; market conditions and quotes can change.

</details>

**Pass gate:** 5/5 and a 20-row quote notebook with accurate dollar conversions. You must never substitute last or midpoint for a guaranteed execution price.

## Module 3 (weeks 9–12): calls, puts, buyers, and sellers

### Lesson

An option is a contract with two sides. The **buyer** or *holder* pays a premium for a right. The **seller** or *writer* receives that premium when opening a short position and accepts an obligation if assigned. For the standard stock options in this chapter, one contract covers 100 shares. A **call** buyer may buy those shares at the strike; a **put** buyer may sell them at the strike. The call writer may have to sell or deliver shares, and the put writer may have to buy them. These rights and obligations are described in the [SEC options bulletin](https://www.investor.gov/introduction-investing/general-resources/news-alerts/alerts-bulletins/investor-bulletins-63) and [OCC disclosure document](https://www.theocc.com/company-information/documents-and-archives/options-disclosure-document).

To learn option arithmetic, hold time still and imagine the moment of expiration. A call's **intrinsic value** per share is `max(stock price − strike, 0)`. A put's is `max(strike − stock price, 0)`. The `max(..., 0)` part says the holder need not exercise a right that has no favorable intrinsic value. **Profit** then subtracts the premium paid by a buyer or adds the premium received by a writer. Before expiration, an option can have **extrinsic value** on top of intrinsic value because time and uncertain future moves still matter. So an expiration break-even price is neither a forecast nor the price where you must sell before expiration.

Work through a call slowly. ABC is $100 today. You pay $3 per share for one $105 call: `$3 × 100 = $300` leaves your account. If ABC ends at $112, the right to buy at $105 is worth `$7 × 100 = $700`; subtract $300 and your expiration profit is $400 before fees. If ABC ends at $106, the right is worth $100 and the profit is **negative $200**. A correct prediction that the stock would rise was not enough. The expiration break-even is `$105 + $3 = $108`. Below the strike the call's intrinsic value is zero and the premium can be lost in full. A put works in the opposite stock direction: a $95 put costing $2 has a $93 expiration break-even. At a stock price of $88, it is worth `$7 × 100 = $700`, leaving $500 after its $200 premium.

Now reverse the position. If someone **writes an uncovered $105 call** for $3, $300 is the most premium they can keep from that call.
