Fictional quotes and probability inputs are teaching assumptions, not observed returns or market forecasts.

## Primary sources checked for this review

| Subject | Source and supported scope |
| --- | --- |
| Options rights and risks | [SEC options bulletin](https://www.investor.gov/introduction-investing/general-resources/news-alerts/alerts-bulletins/investor-bulletins-63), [OCC disclosure document](https://www.theocc.com/company-information/documents-and-archives/options-disclosure-document). Standard stock-option rights, premiums and risk; check exact series for expiry conventions. |
| Exercise and assignment | [OIC exercise FAQ](https://www.optionseducation.org/referencelibrary/faq/options-exercise), [OIC exercise overview](https://www.optionseducation.org/optionsoverview/exercising-options), [FINRA assignment](https://www.finra.org/investors/insights/trading-options-understanding-assignment). Early assignment, clearing-member exercise-by-exception, broker exceptions, single-leg exposure and after-hours risk. |
| Pricing and Greeks | [OIC pricing](https://www.optionseducation.org/optionsoverview/options-pricing), [delta](https://www.optionseducation.org/advancedconcepts/delta), [gamma](https://www.optionseducation.org/advancedconcepts/gamma), [theta](https://www.optionseducation.org/advancedconcepts/theta), [vega](https://www.optionseducation.org/advancedconcepts/vega). Intrinsic/extrinsic value and local sensitivity estimates, with other inputs held fixed. |
| Adjustments and product differences | [OIC splits](https://www.optionseducation.org/news/splits-happen), [Cboe specifications](https://www.cboe.com/tradable_products/sp_500/spx_weekly_options/specifications). Premium multipliers and deliverables are separate; exercise style and settlement depend on the exact product and expiration. |
| Margin transition | [FINRA Notice 26-10](https://www.finra.org/rules-guidance/notices/26-10). Effective June 4, 2026, with a broker transition through October 20, 2027; verify the broker's actual implementation. |
| Tax reference | [IRS Publication550](https://www.irs.gov/publications/p550). Available 2025 edition; classification and taxpayer circumstances matter. The course does not assign personalized tax treatment. |
| Paper trading | [IBKR documentation](https://www.ibkrguides.com/orgportal/aboutpapertradingaccount.htm), [CME simulator FAQ](https://www.cmegroup.com/articles/faqs/trading-simulator-faq.html). Access and simulation limitations; CME is an adjacent futures-options tool, not the beginner equity-options practice requirement. |
| Historical quote conventions | [Cboe interval product](https://datashop.cboe.com/option-quote-intervals). Product-specific fields and quote-size conventions; no licensed historical dataset was purchased or independently audited. |
| Web application stack | [Cloudflare framework guide](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/framework-guides/web-apps/nextjs/). Vinext supplies a Next.js compatible API surface on Vite/Workers. The app uses React, TypeScript, D1, Drizzle and server-side validation. |

Sources can contain simplified or dated generalizations. The course therefore asks the learner to use a contract's actual expiry, settlement and adjustment terms. It does not repeat a universal monthly expiration day, broker cutoff, paper-fill rule or margin minimum.

## Executable laboratory checks

All bundled market inputs are explicitly synthetic. Fixed backward entry/exit chronology, boolean/fractional quantity acceptance, negative elapsed time and negative liquidation haircuts that could falsely improve a stress result. Added regression cases. The 20 lab tests pass; the demo reproduces D1=$38 and D2=−$42 under the fictional base assumptions. Independent arithmetic checked 1,200 generated payoff cases over three seeds. Fixture hashes match and the final synthetic forecast segment remains reserved by the default report. Hashes attest file identity, not market truth.

## Application checks

The application contains database migrations and real authenticated API routes for progress, notes, preferences, quizzes, reviews and JSON/CSV exports. The server, rather than the browser, validates sequence and computes checkpoint scores. Each read and write is scoped to the platform's user ID. The two forms contain 80 question instances altogether. Tests independently check answer text and arithmetic, response validation, review intervals and CSV escaping. Local integration, browser and build results are recorded below after execution.

The source importer validates 64 consecutive lesson IDs in 8 modules, retains teaching prefaces and keeps checkpoint text separate from individual lessons. The local-link checker excludes dependency and generated directories.

## Limits

Paid courses, gated broker account features, live executions, licensed historical options data and the learner's personal finances were not verified. The app has no broker connection or live price feed. Its payoff chart is an idealized expiration calculation, not a pre-expiration pricing engine. The course's durations, mastery thresholds and review intervals are teaching choices. Passing a course or a synthetic test cannot establish a live trading edge, personal suitability or that a course is the best in the world.

See [the October 26 history](VERIFICATION_HISTORY_2026_10_26.md) for the earlier source audit. Old verification claims retain their original date and scope.

## Application results recorded during this review

| Check | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Node content, quiz, scheduling and export tests | Passing; includes independent canonical answers for all 80 quiz instances and teaching-package integrity. |
| Authenticated local API integration | 39 HTTP checks passed, plus saved-state assertions and a two-user database-isolation check. Original local test-user data restored afterward. |
| Course package | 49 teaching files in a sanitized ZIP; CRC integrity and internal Markdown targets checked. A new blank record is included, and the original personal record is excluded. |
| Python laboratories | 20 tests passed; generated-payoff checks and synthetic fixture integrity also passed. |
| Local references | 344 local Markdown links passed before the final packaging edits; the final validation rechecks the resulting tree. |

Integration exercises cover unauthorized requests, cross-origin writes, invalid content types, note upserts, preferences, sequential completion, checkpoint prerequisites, failed and successful forms, stale-form rejection, recall scheduling and exports. They run only against the local preview database. Production learning records have not been populated with test completions.

## Final browser validation

The desktop and mobile browser smoke passed all 13 stages in a real headless Google Chrome session. It verified note typing without focus loss, explicit saves surviving reload, lesson completion, wrong-answer feedback, an alternate checkpoint pass, recall-review persistence, notebook and resource navigation, study preferences, and payoff inputs. The call and put examples each return $300 before fees and $298 after $2 total fees; negative inputs are rejected. At 390×844, the dashboard, course, reader, practice tool and preferences had no horizontal page overflow and the mobile menu opened and closed. Fresh-page runs reported no JavaScript errors.

The teaching ZIP and Python attachments returned HTTP 200 after restarting the preview; ZIP integrity was checked. Local browser-test records were restored afterward. TypeScript checking and all 13 Node tests passed. The final publication workflow runs the production build against the source state it pushes. Hosted sign-in uses the Sites platform; local browser tests used its documented portable-development mock identity, not the learner's production account.

## Audit corrections and current checks

All 14 findings from the subsequent full audit have been corrected in the course and application source. Requests now use a measured 64 KiB streaming JSON limit, including bodies without Content-Length. The budget accommodates the advertised 10,000-code-unit notes with Unicode and JSON escaping. Quiz submissions use an issued revision and a unique database sequence; concurrent duplicates or stale forms receive a conflict. Recall updates use a conditional revision check so two tabs cannot silently overwrite an acknowledged result.

Due reviews update in an open tab and on focus, visibility, and navigation. Resource and library retries repeat their failed reads. Important assumptions and limitations use 12px text and measured contrast above 6:1; search focus is visible and navigation focuses the content. These checks address specific accessibility defects, not full WCAG conformance.

The Python ledger validates opening and subsequently mutated state before accounting operations. Direct quote sizes reject fractional, boolean, NaN, and infinite values before fill modeling. The research path now branches its evidence requirements by synthetic, published-index, and licensed-contract projects. The learning record points to the correct advanced introduction, zero-bid guidance preserves illiquidity evidence, and Volume 4 includes a qualified calendar no-arbitrage example, share/cash ledger, fresh questions, and pass task.

New checkpoint attempts also retain selected answers, graded feedback, and course/question versions in learning records and exports. The schema migration preserves existing scores and progress; unavailable historical answers remain empty. The importer has a read-only freshness check covering course/library JSON, hosted attachments, and the offline ZIP.

| Current check | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Python laboratories | All 24 tests pass, including invalid opening/mutated ledgers and quote-size regressions. |
| App unit/content/export/quiz checks | All 19 tests pass, including streaming cancellation, Unicode/escaped notes, retained evidence, and detection of stale artifacts without rewriting them. |
| TypeScript and lint | Both pass; lint reports zero errors and warnings. |
| Authenticated local API integration | 49 HTTP status checks plus persistence, grading, concurrent checkpoint/recall conflicts, evidence export, and two-user isolation assertions pass. Test records are restored. |
| Browser integration | All 14 desktop/mobile smoke stages pass, including saves, checkpoints, reviews, attachments, preferences, payoff arithmetic, and no horizontal overflow on the tested screens. Test records are restored. |
| Additional browser regressions | Review time/focus transitions, library/resource retry recovery, visible search focus, and measured text contrast pass with mocked API responses and no database writes. |
| Built Worker runtime | The production artifact serves the home page, health, resources, and ZIP successfully; unsigned learning requests return 401. The nonmutating browser regressions also pass against this built artifact. |
| Migration | Original and appended schemas preserve legacy scores/counts in a temporary SQLite check. Drizzle reports no further schema changes. The appended local migration applies successfully. |
| Package | Fresh snapshots, source/public attachments, and the 49-file ZIP agree; ZIP CRCs pass. |
| Dependency security | The installed full dependency tree, including development tooling, reports zero known advisories in the November 14 npm scan. This does not establish that software is vulnerability-free. |
| Build | The updated React/Vinext/Vite/Cloudflare stack completes the production build. The publication workflow rebuilds after final documentation/snapshot changes and pushes the corresponding source. |

The update uses React/DOM/RSC 19.3.1, Vinext 1.4.5, Vite 8.3.8, Cloudflare Vite plugin 1.69.1, Wrangler 4.162.0, Next compatibility package 16.4.6, and Zod 4.6.7. Compatible transitive overrides resolve the audited dependency alerts; lint, Drizzle generation, browser/runtime behavior, and the build were checked after the update. Framework sourcemap/chunking notices remain build-tool diagnostics and do not constitute a failed build.

No production learning record was used for these test completions. Hosted schema migrations and publication follow the existing private Sites workflow. The course still makes no claim of trading profitability or personal suitability.

title: A small glossary you can use as you learn
body:
# A small glossary you can use as you learn

[Beginner course](beginner/README.md) · [Full library](README.md)

Look up a word when a lesson introduces it. Do not memorize this page before starting. Each definition is a reminder; the linked module supplies examples, qualifications, and sources. Definitions involving shares refer to the course's standard physically settled stock/ETF examples unless otherwise stated.

## Module 1 · Markets

| Term | Plain meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Stock / share | A share is a unit of ownership in a company. Its price can rise or fall. |
| ETF | An exchange-traded fund: a fund whose shares trade on an exchange. Its holdings and risks depend on that fund. |
| Index | A calculated measure of a specified group of securities. A fund tracking an index is a separate investment. |
| Broker | The firm handling your account and routing or executing your orders under its rules. |
| Bid / ask | Bid is a displayed buying offer; ask is a displayed selling offer. Both have a time and limited size. |
| Spread | Ask minus bid. It is one trading-cost consideration, not the complete cost of a trade. |
| Limit order / fill | A limit sets an acceptable buy ceiling or sell floor. A fill is a confirmed execution; submitting the order does not guarantee one. |

[Examples in Module 1](beginner/01_MARKETS.md)

## Module 2 · Contracts

| Term | Plain meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Underlying | The stock, ETF, or other specified asset or reference the option is tied to. |
| Call | A contract giving its holder a right to buy under its terms. A short call has the corresponding obligation if assigned. |
| Put | A contract giving its holder a right to sell under its terms. A short put has the corresponding obligation if assigned. |
| Strike | The contract's exercise price, rather than the option's premium or the stock's current market price. |
| Expiration | The contract's end date. Last trading time and exercise deadlines must be checked separately. |
| Premium / multiplier | Premium is the option's price. The multiplier converts a quote to total dollars: quote × multiplier × contracts. |
| Long / short | Long means you own an option; short means you wrote an open option obligation. Selling an owned option to close it differs from writing a new one. |

[Examples in Module 2](beginner/02_CONTRACTS.md)

## Module 3 · Values and results

| Term | Plain meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Intrinsic value | Immediate exercise value. For a standard call: max(stock − strike, 0); for a put: max(strike − stock, 0), before the multiplier. |
| Profit and loss / P&L | The result after comparing proceeds, payments, liabilities, and stated costs. Premium received alone is not profit. |
| Break-even | The outcome where profit is zero under stated assumptions. An expiration break-even is not a required stock price for an earlier profitable sale. |
| Moneyness / ITM / OTM | How stock price relates to strike. ITM means positive intrinsic value; OTM means no intrinsic value and an unfavorable exercise difference. Neither says what your trade earned. |

[Examples in Module 3](beginner/03_PROFIT.md)

## Module 4 · Changing prices

| Term | Plain meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Extrinsic value | Option premium minus intrinsic value; also called time value. It is not a separate cash payment. |
| Realized volatility | A measure of price movement already observed over a chosen period. |
| Implied volatility / IV | A volatility input inferred from an option quote using a model. It is not a promised future outcome. |
| Delta | A model's local estimate of option-value change per $1 underlying move, with other inputs fixed. |
| Gamma | A model's local estimate of how delta changes when the underlying moves. |
| Theta | A model's estimate of the effect of time passing, often per calendar day. Verify platform units. |
| Vega / rho | Model estimates for IV and interest-rate changes respectively. Common units use a one percentage-point change; verify the platform. |

[Examples in Module 4](beginner/04_PRICES.md)

## Module 5 · Operations

| Term | Plain meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Exercise | Using an option's contractual right. Standard stock-call exercise buys shares; standard stock-put exercise sells shares. |
| Assignment | The writer is required to fulfill a contract that was exercised. A long spread leg does not automatically resolve the resulting shares. |
| American / European style | American permits early exercise under applicable rules; European restricts exercise to the specified expiration time. These do not describe geography. |
| Settlement / deliverable | Settlement describes how obligations are completed. The deliverable specifies shares, cash, or other property due under the contract. |
| Exercise by exception | An OCC clearing-member procedure for expiring options meeting its in-the-money threshold, absent contrary instructions. Broker account procedures can differ. |
| Ex-dividend date | The date determining whether a new share buyer is entitled to the announced distribution under applicable rules. |

[Examples in Module 5](beginner/05_OPERATIONS.md)

## Module 6 · Positions

| Term | Plain meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Covered call | Owned shares plus a short call covering those shares. The stock can still suffer substantial losses, while upside is limited. |
| Protective put | Owned shares plus a matching long put, providing a temporary sale right at the strike for a premium. |
| Cash-secured put | A short put with cash reserved to fund assignment. This funding does not remove the risk of a stock collapse. |
| Vertical spread / debit / credit | A matching-expiration option pair at different strikes. Debit means net cash paid; credit means net cash received. Operational risks remain. |

[Examples in Module 6](beginner/06_STRATEGIES.md)

## Modules 7–8 · Decisions and practice

| Term | Plain meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Expected value | The probability-weighted average of possible outcomes under the stated probabilities. Those probabilities can be wrong. |
| Position size | How many shares or contracts are held. Check the full dollar exposure and obligations before choosing quantity. |
| Correlation / concentration | Positions can move or lose together; several tickers can still carry one large shared risk. |
| Drawdown | A decline from a prior equity high to a later lower value. State whether deposits, withdrawals, and open positions are included. |
| Paper / shadow record | A simulation or written hypothetical decision log. It does not prove live fill quality or profit. |

[Risk examples](beginner/07_RISK.md) · [Paper practice](beginner/08_PRACTICE.md)

These **40 grouped entries** are a lookup aid. Keep adding your own short definitions and changed-number examples to the [workbook](beginner/WORKBOOK.md).

title: Options, one small lesson at a time
body:
# Options, one small lesson at a time

**Start with [Lesson 01: your first goal is understanding](beginner/01_MARKETS.md).** You need no trading experience, brokerage account, coding, or real money. A notebook and ordinary calculator are enough.

This course teaches **U.S. stock and ETF options** from zero in **64 small lessons across 8 modules**. The default is **10–15 minutes per study day, five days a week**. Read one lesson, work its example, try the new question, and explain the idea in your own words before opening the answer. Use the remaining minutes for recall. If the lesson takes longer, split it across sessions.

The [84-session review plan](beginner/REVIEW_PLAN.md) includes 64 lesson sessions, 8 module checkpoints, and 12 review sessions. At five sessions a week it occupies about **17 weeks before extra retries or split sessions**. This is a planning example, not a deadline or a promise of readiness. Repeat an idea until you can explain it. Completing this course measures learning; it does not establish a profitable strategy or approve live trading.

## Your route

| Module | Lessons | What you will be able to do |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [1. Money and markets](beginner/01_MARKETS.md) | 01–08 | Read a basic quote, calculate share cost, and explain a limit order. |
| [2. The option contract](beginner/02_CONTRACTS.md) | 09–16 | Identify a call or put and calculate its premium in dollars. |
| [3. Profit and loss](beginner/03_PROFIT.md) | 17–24 | Separate exercise value, moneyness, profit, and writer obligations. |
| [4. Why prices change](beginner/04_PRICES.md) | 25–32 | Explain time, volatility, and local Greek estimates without calling them guarantees. |
| [5. Account operations](beginner/05_OPERATIONS.md) | 33–40 | Follow cash and shares through closing, exercise, assignment, and expiration. |
| [6. Position structures](beginner/06_STRATEGIES.md) | 41–48 | Explain seven common structures and why complexity or a trade may be unnecessary. |
| [7. Risk and decisions](beginner/07_RISK.md) | 49–56 | Account for losses, position size, uncertainty, and shared risk. |
| [8. Put it together](beginner/08_PRACTICE.md) | 57–64 | Keep an honest paper record and complete small operational cases. |

Every lesson has a worked example, a fresh question, and a folded explanation. Every module has a checkpoint with a separate folded key. Save your first answer before checking. Correct every funding, share, expiry, and order-status error; a correct guess without an explanation is a prompt to review.

## Keep the first day small

Open Lesson 01, read the example, answer its question, and write one sentence explaining what you learned. Stop there if your study time is up. You do not need to open the rest of this library today.

Use these when you need them:

- [Plain-language glossary](beginner/GLOSSARY.md): look up one term after meeting it in a lesson; no first-day memorization.
- [Workbook](beginner/WORKBOOK.md): copy only the block needed for today's work.
- [Review plan](beginner/REVIEW_PLAN.md): find your next session and revisit older ideas.
- [Browser app source and setup](course-app/README.md): the frontend/backend implementation of the course. Follow its setup instructions to run the app; a source folder is not a hosted URL.
- [Full course library](README.md): source verification, reference volumes, and optional deeper study.

## Scope and expectations

Prices, symbols, probabilities, fills, and accounts in exercises are invented unless explicitly identified as real dated observations. Most arithmetic starts with $0 teaching fees so you can learn one idea; real trading must include costs and exact contract terms. Advanced math and Python are optional extensions. You can finish with a well-reasoned decision to continue observing or not trade options.

Mechanics are checked against the SEC, OCC/OIC, FINRA, and exchange specifications. Read the [verification report](VERIFICATION_REPORT.md) for what was checked and what remains account-specific. The [OCC disclosure document](https://www.theocc.com/company-information/documents-and-archives/options-disclosure-document) explains the official characteristics and risks and must be read before actual options trading.

[Begin Lesson 01](beginner/01_MARKETS.md) · [Return to full library](README.md)

title: A flexible plan for 84 small sessions
body:
# A flexible plan for 84 small sessions

[Beginner course](beginner/README.md) · [Workbook](beginner/WORKBOOK.md) · [Full library](README.md)

The planning baseline is **64 new-lesson sessions + 8 checkpoint sessions + 12 review sessions = 84 sessions**. At **five 10–15 minute sessions per week**, that is 16 full weeks plus 4 sessions, or **about 17 weeks**. Retries, rest days, split lessons, and capstone work can add sessions. There is no completion deadline or promised date of trading readiness.

On a lesson day, allow roughly 5–10 minutes to read, reproduce the example, and answer; use 3–5 minutes for recall. Stop at your time limit and resume where you left off. The four small capstone cases in Lesson 63 may need separate sessions. Split any checkpoint taking longer than 15 minutes; keep the saved first attempt and continue the next day.

## The sequence

| Module | New lessons | Review sessions | Checkpoint | Planning sessions |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | ---: |
| [1. Markets](beginner/01_MARKETS.md) | 01–08 | One after Lesson 04; one after 08 | Module 1 checkpoint after the second review | 11 |
| [2. Contracts](beginner/02_CONTRACTS.md) | 09–16 | One after Lesson 12 | Module 2 checkpoint after Lesson 16 | 10 |
| [3. Profit](beginner/03_PROFIT.md) | 17–24 | One after Lesson 20; one after 24 | Module 3 checkpoint after the second review | 11 |
| [4. Prices](beginner/04_PRICES.md) | 25–32 | One after Lesson 28 | Module 4 checkpoint after Lesson 32 | 10 |
| [5. Operations](beginner/05_OPERATIONS.md) | 33–40 | One after Lesson 36; one after 40 | Module 5 checkpoint after the second review | 11 |
| [6. Strategies](beginner/06_STRATEGIES.md) | 41–48 | One after Lesson 44 | Module 6 checkpoint after Lesson 48 | 10 |
| [7. Risk](beginner/07_RISK.md) | 49–56 | One after Lesson 52; one after 56 | Module 7 checkpoint after the second review | 11 |
| [8. Practice](beginner/08_PRACTICE.md) | 57–64 | One after Lesson 60 | Module 8 checkpoint after Lesson 64 | 10 |
| **Total** | **64** | **12** | **8** | **84** |

The table specifies the order, not calendar dates. Missed days do not become extra homework for tomorrow. Resume the next small session.

## Make reviews spaced

At the start or end of each study session, spend a minute recalling one earlier idea without notes. Revisit a lesson approximately **1, 3, and 7 study days** after learning it; exact spacing can shift around your schedule. These brief recalls are inside the daily time budget. The 12 dedicated review sessions provide longer cumulative practice.

For a dedicated review, choose three questions: one from recent lessons, one older question, and one item you previously missed. Change at least one number in a calculation. Explain units and cash/share changes. Check only after preserving your answer. Spend the remaining time correcting one weak idea; avoid rereading an entire module passively.

Example after Lesson 20: recall why a bid differs from an ask, calculate a new 100-multiplier premium, then solve a fresh put-profit case. This combines old and recent knowledge.

## Advance when the idea is clear

Each module's checkpoint gives its specific standard. For a missed concept, reread the relevant lesson and solve a changed case next study day. Correct every cash, multiplier, share, exercise/assignment, expiration, and order-status error before moving to material that depends on it. Keep original answers and later retries distinct in the [workbook](beginner/WORKBOOK.md).

If ordinary percentages or dollar units remain difficult, pause for the relevant portion of the [math bridge](FOUNDATION_MATH_BRIDGE.md). If a lesson feels easy, still answer its fresh question and explain why the answer follows. Coding and advanced pricing formulas are optional later study.

## After the final session

Choose a small next step: repeat weak lessons, observe dated chains without orders, keep a paper decision log, study a particular portfolio question, or begin an optional deeper module. A decision not to trade is valid. Course completion, checkpoint scores, and simulated gains do not provide broker approval, personal suitability, or proof of a live edge.

[Start Lesson 01](beginner/01_MARKETS.md)

title: Your small daily workbook
body:
# Your small daily workbook

[Beginner course](beginner/README.md) · [Review plan](beginner/REVIEW_PLAN.md) · [Full library](README.md)

Copy the block needed today into your notebook or a new file. You do not need to complete every template at once. Keep first attempts alongside corrections; an error is useful learning evidence. The existing [learning record](MY_LEARNING_RECORD.md) remains preserved; these blocks do not assert any prior skills or assessment passes.

## 1. Daily lesson card · use from Lesson 01

```text
Study date and lesson number:
Today's one idea, in my own words:
My first try-it answer and calculation (before viewing the key):
What I got right:
Correction, if needed, and why:
One sentence explaining the answer aloud:
Next small step or changed-number retry:
Recall dates: next study day / after 3 study days / after 7 study days
```

Do not give yourself a pass for copying the explanation. A better check is a new number or a short explanation without looking.

## 2. Recall and checkpoint card

```text
Lesson/module reviewed:
Question I answered without notes:
My saved answer:
Check against key: correct / partly correct / not yet
If wrong, mistaken idea (units, sign, cash, shares, timing, or definition):
Corrected reasoning:
Fresh retry question and scheduled study day:
Fresh answer and result:
Funding/expiry/assignment/order-status errors all corrected? yes/no
```

For a checkpoint that takes more than 15 minutes, save the work and continue next session. Correct cash/share and operational errors before advancing to material that relies on them.

## 3. Quote notebook · use after learning quote fields

Observation is enough. No order or brokerage deposit is required. If collecting actual quotes, use a legally available source and identify delayed data as delayed.

```text
Observation date/time and time zone:
Source and source quote time; known data delay:
Underlying symbol and observed underlying price/time:
Exact option series: call/put, strike, expiration date, adjustment/root:
Premium multiplier and deliverable; specification or memo source:
Bid / ask; displayed sizes if available:
Last trade and its timestamp, if provided:
Spread per quote unit and dollars per one contract:
Known event or corporate action; facts not checked yet:
What this observation shows:
What it cannot prove about execution or future profit:
```

If a field is unavailable, write **unknown**. A missing timestamp is not permission to call a quote current.

## 4. Fictional paper ticket · use after the operations module

```text
SIMULATION ONLY — no live order submitted
Decision date/time and time zone:
Exercise or observation source (invented case / dated quote):
Exact underlying and option terms; quantity for every leg:
Action: buy/sell to open/close; multiplier and deliverable:
Why this position? What would reject the idea?
Compare with: cash / shares / simpler position / no trade
Exercise style and settlement; actual expiry and last trading time:
Events and broker rules known / unknown:
Observed bid/ask and quote age; order limit and validity:
Fee assumptions; adverse-fill assumption; nonfill handling:
Cash paid/received; modeled loss; share/funding/assignment case:
Hypothetical practice limit; does one whole contract fit?
Exit and expiry plan, including deadlines needing confirmation:
Decision: simulate / wait / no trade; reason:
```

For a fictional case, use only the fills expressly supplied. For a shadow observation, label hypothetical fills as assumptions. You cannot infer a passive limit fill just because the market later moved favorably.

## 5. Cash and position ledger

Copy rows as events occur. Use positive shares for owned stock and negative shares for short stock. Use positive option quantity for a long option and negative for an open short. Cash is not the same as equity.

| Time/event | Confirmed order status | Cash change | Cash balance | Shares | Each option quantity | Mark/source | Account equity |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- | --- | ---: |
| Start | No open orders | 0 |  | 0 | None |  |  |
| Entry | Filled / partial / unfilled / unknown |  |  |  |  |  |  |
| Later event |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
| Close or settlement |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |

In a simple case, **equity = cash + share market value + long-option value − short-option liability**. Multiply shares by the stated stock mark; multiply option quotes by quantity and their actual multiplier. A market mark estimates value; a fill determines an executed cash flow. Track external deposits/withdrawals separately if they exist.

## 6. Assignment and expiration rehearsal

```text
Exact option and relevant product rules:
Position before event: cash / shares / options / pending orders:
Event: exercise / assignment / expiry / cash settlement / unknown status
Shares received or delivered (with sign):
Strike cash payment or receipt:
Earlier premium and fees, kept separate:
Which option disappeared? Which still exists?
Funding/margin and dividend consequences in this case:
Resulting positions and equity under the stated marks:
Any later stock-price exposure or open order?
Broker deadline/procedure that a real case would require:
What evidence would confirm that the account is resolved?
```

A spread's long option remains a separate position unless the case or actual confirmed instruction says otherwise. A submitted cancellation is not a confirmed cancellation. For fuller practice use the [operational casebook](OPERATIONAL_CASEBOOK.md).

## 7. A complete no-trade entry

```text
Date and observation:
Idea considered:
Reason to abstain (unclear term / large contract / wide spread / event / no signal / other):
Known facts supporting that reason:
What remains unknown:
Useful next learning step:
No trade submitted; no trade P&L claimed:
```

You do not need to invent a trade to fill the workbook. A clear abstention is a recorded decision.

## 8. Five-minute weekly review

```text
Lessons actually completed and still needing a retry:
One explanation I can now give without notes:
One repeated error and how I will change my practice:
Any simulated fill, cost, or position assumption I overstated:
Next study session and one older lesson to recall:
```

Keep the weekly review about learning and accounting. A profitable fictional result does not erase a process mistake.

title: Options Academy application
body:
# Options Academy application

A complete beginner learning app for U.S. stock and ETF options. The course contains 64 short lessons, 8 module checkpoints with 2 quiz forms, daily recall reviews, notes, an educational expiration-payoff chart and a reference library. Default study time is 15 minutes. Course completion does not establish trading profitability.

## Advanced Academy

Open **Advanced academy** in the classroom navigation. The advanced program brings the 26-module curriculum into the app with teaching sections, original staged decision cases, portfolio mandates, exhibits, submission examples, analytic rubrics, assignments, defense prompts, and primary references. Module 10 is the flagship Trade Design seminar. Beginner and advanced module numbers identify separate pathways.

The learning loop is: prepare → make an initial recommendation → save the initial submission → consider new information → revise → compare with the debrief → practice on a changed case → return for a later check. Numeric checks are server-graded practice. Written submissions are preserved for rubric review; saving writing does not automatically grade its reasoning or certify mastery. Generated practice variants exercise known question families and do not constitute an independently administered unseen examination. The program has not yet been validated in a learner pilot.

Advanced records use separate user-scoped D1 tables. Every save appends an immutable draft/submission revision and the course packet it used. Unique owner/module/revision indexes prevent competing tabs from silently replacing work. Practice stores the response, expected result, explanation and question version, with a unique owner/module/sequence key preventing replayed submissions. The advanced evidence JSON export includes historical course snapshots. These records are separate from beginner JSON/CSV exports.

The laboratories cover equal-budget portfolio comparisons, European theoretical prices and sensitivities, a short-leg assignment ledger and a supplied partial-fill/cancellation episode. Inputs and episodes are fictional teaching assumptions. Model prices, local sensitivities, expiration values and supplied fills have distinct meanings. All labs provide readable tables and explanations.

The canonical advanced teaching source is `content/graduate.json`. Source changes require incrementing `GRADUATE_VERSION` in `lib/graduate.ts`; changes to question interpretation or key logic also require incrementing `GRADUATE_QUESTION_VERSION`. Existing records preserve their prior versions. `content:import` renders the full advanced Markdown download and inserts it into the library and offline ZIP. The ordinary source freshness check detects stale rendered copies.

Advanced API contracts:

| Route | Behavior |
| --- | --- |
| GET /api/graduate | Read only the current learner's submission history and numeric practice |
| PUT /api/graduate | Append a draft or submitted revision with optimistic concurrency checking |
| GET /api/graduate/practice?moduleId=10 | Request the next module-specific numeric practice variant without answer keys |
| POST /api/graduate/practice | Validate, independently derive answers, and atomically save feedback |
| GET /api/graduate/export | Export the learner's advanced evidence and historical content packets |

Run `node --experimental-strip-types tests/graduate-api.integration.mjs` against a local authenticated development service after applying migrations. It exercises isolation, immutable first attempts, concurrent requests, validation, answer-key handling and exports, then restores portable test records. Run this separately from other tests that write the portable learner's records.

## Application design

### Adaptive teaching, review and pilot

Open **Advanced academy → Teaching studio**. The tutor uses saved error evidence, prerequisites and due checks to recommend study. It provides a single question, specific diagnosis, hints, worked correction and a changed transfer check. Assistance and original answers remain in immutable event history. It is a deterministic instructional system; it does not make an external language-model call.

Writing feedback evaluates an exact saved submission against its module's rubric. It quotes detectable argument evidence, identifies missing working/alternatives/uncertainty, flags selected explicit contradictions and provides module-specific revision questions. Detected evidence is not an academic grade. The review desk downloads the original packet and records actual criterion scores, exact quoted evidence, reviewer challenge and learner response. External reviews are attributed reports, not credential verification.

The pilot enrolls with explicit consent and prior-experience context, fingerprints the question/answer/grading blueprint, records an actual baseline and schedules server-enforced day-7 and day-30 forms. Day-7 closes at elapsed day 14 and day-30 at day 45; late/missing measurements are visible. Forms are parallel numerical practice; the full written-case/reviewer protocol lives in the teaching library. Confidence and assistance are retained with every new assessment. All reviewers’ original ratings remain visible, with a distinct-rater calibration view. No cohort outcomes are invented. Normal teaching reads load latest cumulative snapshots, and the full export streams historical records in bounded batches.

Additional labs cover joint portfolio shocks/funding and research-evidence critique. **My evidence** includes a capstone artifact manifest with immutable revisions for protocols, data audits, models, execution, stress and defenses.

The additive `drizzle/0003_workable_whirlwind.sql` migration creates owner-scoped teaching events. Apply it once after migrations 0000–0002 in a local database; hosted publication applies pending tracked migrations. The new routes are `/api/teaching`, `/api/teaching/tutor`, `/api/teaching/feedback`, `/api/teaching/review`, `/api/teaching/pilot`, `/api/teaching/artifact` and `/api/teaching/export`. Mutations authenticate, validate a measured JSON body and preserve optimistic revisions. Run `tests/teaching-api.integration.mjs` separately from other tests that write the portable learner's records.

| Layer | Technology | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| UI | React 19 and TypeScript | Responsive dashboard and focused lesson reader |
| Styles | Tailwind CSS 4 and custom CSS | Accessible typography, mobile layouts and clear states |
| Runtime | Vinext, Vite and Cloudflare Workers | Next.js compatible server rendering and API route handlers |
| Database | Cloudflare D1 and Drizzle ORM | Persistent user-scoped progress, notes, preferences and quiz attempts |
| Authentication | Sites ChatGPT sign-in | Platform-managed identity and private access |
| Validation | Zod | Server validation of every write |
| Content | Markdown imported to committed JSON | Reviewable lessons and source references without a runtime filesystem |
| Tests | Node test runner and Playwright | Independent quiz mathematics, scheduling, content checks and browser/API exercises |

Vinext implements the Next.js API surface on Vite. It is not the Next.js production runtime. Cloudflare documents it for full-stack Workers applications: [official framework guide](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/framework-guides/web-apps/nextjs/). Versions are pinned by package-lock.json.

All learning records are stored in D1, not browser storage. Local previews and the hosted app use separate databases. User keys come from trusted platform identity, and each read and write filters by that user. Notes are rendered as text; course Markdown does not enable raw HTML. Mutation requests validate origin, exact JSON content type, and a measured 64 KiB streaming body limit, including requests without Content-Length. Notes accept up to 10,000 JavaScript string code units, including Unicode and JSON-escaped controls within that request budget.

The server calculates quiz scores, checks completion order and module prerequisites, and stores attempts. A unique per-user/module attempt sequence atomically accepts each issued quiz revision once; stale or concurrent duplicate submissions receive 409. New attempts retain selected answers, graded feedback, and course/question versions in learning records and exports. Older attempts keep their original scores, with unavailable historical answer evidence left empty. The two quiz forms alternate; once seen, they are review practice rather than unseen assessment. Recall updates use a separate revision check so two tabs cannot overwrite an acknowledged review.

## Run locally

Install Node.js 22.13 or newer. Node24 was used during development. From this directory:

```sh
npm run install:ci
npm run lint
npm run typecheck
npm test
npm run build
```

The tracked hosting manifest declares the DB binding. Apply pending local schema migrations in filename order once per local database. A fresh database needs all four migrations. Apply only the migrations not already present in an existing local database:

```sh
node --import ./scripts/sites-env.mjs ./node_modules/wrangler/bin/wrangler.js d1 execute DB --local --config dist/server/wrangler.json --persist-to .wrangler/state --file drizzle/0000_loving_thanos.sql
node --import ./scripts/sites-env.mjs ./node_modules/wrangler/bin/wrangler.js d1 execute DB --local --config dist/server/wrangler.json --persist-to .wrangler/state --file drizzle/0001_modern_firestar.sql
node --import ./scripts/sites-env.mjs ./node_modules/wrangler/bin/wrangler.js d1 execute DB --local --config dist/server/wrangler.json --persist-to .wrangler/state --file drizzle/0002_regular_karen_page.sql
node --import ./scripts/sites-env.mjs ./node_modules/wrangler/bin/wrangler.js d1 execute DB --local --config dist/server/wrangler.json --persist-to .wrangler/state --file drizzle/0003_workable_whirlwind.sql
npm run dev -- --port 5173
```

Visit the printed loopback URL. Select **Sign in with ChatGPT**. Portable development simulates sign-in with a local test user; no external account or secrets are required. Production does not include that mock identity. The dev server and local migrations share .wrangler/state. Do not apply a migration again to the same database.

Builds and local preview require network access when dependencies are not cached. The app itself does not request a market data feed or connect to a brokerage.

## Backend endpoints

| Method and path | Behavior |
| --- | --- |
| GET /api/learning | Authenticated profile, progress, notes and attempts |
| POST /api/progress | Complete the next lesson, or log a recall using its current reviewRevision |
| PUT /api/notes | Save one lesson note, up to 10,000 JavaScript string code units |
| PUT /api/profile | Save daily study minutes and an IANA timezone |
| GET /api/quiz?moduleId=1 | Get the next checkpoint form and revision after completing its lessons |
| POST /api/quiz | Validate five exact answer keys and the issued revision, grade and atomically persist one attempt |
| GET /api/export | Download the current user's learning record as JSON |
| GET /api/export?format=csv | Download a spreadsheet-safe CSV learning record |
| GET /api/health | Check runtime database readiness without revealing user data |

A new account has no completions or quiz results. Lessons may be previewed freely. Completion requires the preceding lesson and the preceding module's checkpoint. A checkpoint passes at 5/5. Review intervals are 1, 3, 7, 14 and 30 days after successive recalls; a miss schedules another review in one day. Due reviews update in an open tab every 30 seconds and on focus, visibility, and navigation. The app supplies an illustrative self-study schedule, not notifications or automated trading.

## Update the course

The source lessons live in the parent beginner directory. After editing source material, regenerate the committed content snapshot from this checkout:

```sh
npm run content:import
npm run content:check
npm run lint
npm test
npm run typecheck
npm run build
```

An independently deployed checkout can build from the committed content JSON without the parent repository. Regeneration and the read-only freshness check need the parent Markdown files. The importer requires exactly 8 modules and 64 ordered lessons and copies the reference library for in-app reading. `content:check` compares the course/library snapshots, hosted Python/data attachments, and offline ZIP without repairing or rewriting a stale artifact.

When changing the database, edit db/schema.ts and run npm run db:generate. Inspect and retain the generated SQL and Drizzle metadata. Migrations change schema only; content is bundled with the application. Sites applies pending hosted migrations during publication. Never edit an applied migration.

## Verification and deployment

See the parent [verification report](VERIFICATION_REPORT.md) for the exact checks and their limits. Browser tests use an installed Chromium-compatible browser; development used Google Chrome on macOS. The source includes test scripts; screenshots and local runtime state are ignored and are not production user data.

With the local preview running, execute `node --experimental-strip-types tests/api.integration.mjs`, then `node tests/browser.integration.mjs` separately; each restores its original portable test-user records. `node tests/ui-regressions.integration.mjs` uses mocked API responses and tests review time transitions, failed-read retries, contrast, and search focus without database writes. Tests also cover streamed-body cancellation, Unicode notes, concurrent quiz/review submissions, migration preservation, answer evidence, and content freshness.

Security updates pin a compatible React/Vinext/Vite/Cloudflare stack. The transitive overrides in package.json keep known vulnerable parser/build-tool versions out of the lockfile; review them with dependency updates, and validate Drizzle generation, lint, the build, and local runtime behavior after changing them. `npm audit` covers development tooling as well as direct production dependencies.

Publishing uses the Sites workflow and the exact project_id in .openai/hosting.json. Preserve the private audience, push the source corresponding to the built artifact, save that version, and deploy it. Never commit credentials, .env files, local databases or .sites-runtime. Production database backups and organizational retention are platform operations; JSON/CSV export gives the learner a portable copy of their own record.

Validation preparation now includes four checked parallel written cases, a learner ZIP containing separate initial/update packets without instructor keys, an external expert review brief and a rating/report template. Read `VALIDATION_READINESS.md` in the Resource library for the owner’s decision to recruit participants later and the AI-assisted audit scope. No human approval or participant outcome is prefilled.

title: Executable options research apprenticeship
body:
# Executable options research apprenticeship

**All data in this directory are synthetic teaching data.** The symbols, quotes, forecasts, P&L, and dates were invented. The program does not connect to a broker or price feed. Its outputs establish whether the stated rules and accounting are internally consistent; they cannot establish a market edge or live fill rate.

This lab is for a learner who can already program in Python. If programming is new, first complete [Sprint 15](LESSONS_03_QUANT.md). Work each arithmetic example by hand before checking it in code. Use Python 3.10 or newer; the project uses only the standard library.

From the project root, run:

```sh
python3 -m unittest discover -s labs -v
python3 labs/options_lab.py
```

The first command checks accounting, timing, pricing, research, and stress behaviors. The second runs the teaching report with the final forecast segment reserved. Only after fixing and dating a research rule should you run `python3 labs/options_lab.py --open-final`. Treat opening that segment as one evaluation of the frozen rule; a later change requires new forward observations.

## Inputs and their boundaries

| File | Use |
| --- | --- |
| [manifest.json](labs/data/manifest.json) | Synthetic source statement, contract terms, assumptions, split, and SHA-256 hashes. `check_manifest()` stops if a fixture changes without a new manifest. |
| [quotes.csv](labs/data/quotes.csv) | Fictional quotes with offset-aware times, bid/ask, sizes, one crossed row, and one zero-bid row. |
| [decisions.csv](labs/data/decisions.csv) | Six prewritten fictional long-call decisions, including a nonfill and a rejected quote. |
| [daily_observations.csv](labs/data/daily_observations.csv) | Twelve development and six validation rows of separate invented forecast and portfolio observations. These are **not** the P&L generated from `decisions.csv`. |
| [final_observations.csv](labs/data/final_observations.csv) | Six reserved fictional forecast outcomes. Open only after writing the forecast evaluation rule. |
| [trial_log.csv](labs/data/trial_log.csv) | An example of recording all three attempted variants, including poor validation results. Extend your own copy for further trials. |

`options_lab.py` checks a SHA-256 hash for each fixture, but hashes prove only that these particular files have not changed. They do not attest to market accuracy, vendor quality, or independent provenance. One crossed quote and one zero-bid quote exercise the classroom policy for unusable fills. A real zero bid can be genuine illiquidity; flag it and retain the raw observation and any held position rather than deleting its loss or inventing an exit. Visible size merely caps an illustrative assumed fill; queue position, routing, hidden liquidity, and adverse selection are not modeled. [IBKR's simulator documentation](https://www.ibkrguides.com/orgportal/aboutpapertradingaccount.htm) also identifies fill and combination-order limitations in paper trading.

The code uses Python floating-point arithmetic for concise classroom examples and rounds report fields for display. A real cash ledger should use integer cents or decimal arithmetic and reconcile every broker cash flow. The `toy_backtest` sample is restricted to one standard 100-multiplier fictional call; an open option is kept as an exposure with no finished P&L.

## Build skill in small steps

1. **Payoff and exercise ledger, beginning during the foundation lessons.** Use `Contract`, `expiration_profit`, and `Ledger`. Hand-check a standard $105 call bought for $3 at a $112 expiry value. Then sell one $100 call for $3 in a hypothetical $10,000 account and assign it at $110. The program must leave short shares and the corresponding cash, not simply erase the option. Try an adjusted 10-share deliverable with a 100 premium multiplier. The program handles a share-only adjusted deliverable; an actual adjustment can also involve cash or another asset, which requires the exact [OCC memo](https://infomemo.theocc.com/infomemo/search-memo).
2. **Pricing and model limits, after probability and replication.** Reproduce the $7.9656 European call value for `S=K=100`, one year, zero rate, and 20% volatility. Compare finite-difference delta with a smaller and larger step. Check put-call parity for matching European calls and puts. Invert the price of a $90 call; the implied-volatility routine expands its bracket instead of assuming volatility cannot exceed 300%. Compare an American put tree with the European put and check convergence as the tree gains steps. Use `call_slice_violations` on three same-expiry strikes; treat violations in *quotes* with care because non-synchronous or wide markets can create apparent violations.
3. **Quote QA and chronology.** Use `quote_flags` and `select_quote` to explain why two of the 13 quote rows are rejected. A valid decision requires a signal timestamp before the selected quote and an order time after it. The selected quote may be no more than five minutes old in this exercise. Change a quote so the latest row is crossed; the code should reject that decision instead of silently taking an earlier favorable row. Real product data require vendor-specific validation and corporate-action rules; [Cboe describes the fields and changing quote-size convention in one historical product](https://datashop.cboe.com/option-quote-intervals).
4. **Order and backtest accounting.** Run `toy_backtest` under optimistic, base, and adverse assumptions. For the base case, D1 is `(2.60−2.20)×100−$2=$38`; D2 is `−$42`. D5 has no entry fill, and D6 has no usable entry quote. Write down why each remains in the decision ledger. Change the entry limit or size and note how a nonfill or partial fill changes your outcome. An open residual position retains its entry price, cash outlay, and quantity for marking and review; this tiny demonstration intentionally does not compute P&L for an unclosed option. A midpoint fill is only an optimistic assumption here.
5. **Forecasts, dependent observations, and selection.** Before examining `final_observations.csv`, write the event definition, forecast date, Brier-score calculation, development baseline, chosen variant, primary outcome, and rejection rule. The example baseline is `5/12 ≈ 0.4167`, computed from development rows only. The toy report keeps the six final rows separate. Compare independent-observation uncertainty with `block_bootstrap_mean_interval`; vary block length and report how your conclusion changes. A moving-block calculation on 18 artificial observations does not justify a population claim. Use `label_event` to exclude a trade whose outcome crosses a development/validation boundary and preserve all variants in the trial log.
6. **Portfolio stress.** Build a hypothetical long call, put, or vertical portfolio using `stress_portfolio`. Show at least eight joint changes in stock price, volatility, elapsed time, and liquidation spread. The function reprices standard European options with one volatility input and an explicit haircut. Separately use `Ledger` to show possible shares and cash after assignment. This is a classroom stress engine: it does not compute broker margin, actual early exercise likelihood, a volatility surface, or executable liquidation prices.

The implementation rejects exit decisions dated before entry, fractional or boolean contract quantities, nonfinite opening cash, invalid displayed sizes, negative elapsed days, and negative liquidation haircuts. `Ledger` validates opening balances and rechecks its public methods, so direct field edits cannot silently create a fractional contract settlement. It models signed whole-share positions; fractional-share balances and cash-in-lieu adjustments need a separate explicit model. Failed validations leave balances unchanged. Quote sizes must be non-boolean integers, and zero/negative visible size blocks an assumed fill. Premium multipliers and adjusted share deliverables remain separate contract fields. A haircut is a cost subtracted from modeled value; entering it as a negative number would incorrectly improve the reported liquidation value. Zero stock value and zero volatility remain valid boundary scenarios.

The suggested record for each stage is: original hand calculation, code output, assumptions, failing counterexample, corrected result, and a one-paragraph explanation. A passing run of the supplied tests shows that the reference implementation behaves as specified on those tests. To pass a course gate, add an unseen case and explain the result without relying on the reference output.

## Three feasible capstone levels

| Evidence level | Appropriate project | Defensible conclusion |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A. Simulator validation | Extend these fictional inputs with adjustments, rejected quotes, funding and assignment tests. | The code follows its specified rules on audited cases. No market-performance inference. |
| B. Published-index analysis | Compare a published options index with a matched published benchmark, documenting methodology, dates, financing, and what the index assumed. | A descriptive comparison of published histories. It does not reconstruct executable option trades. |
| C. Historical contract replay | Use licensed point-in-time option quotes, product specifications, underlying prices, corporate actions, fees, and documented fill rules. | A conditional historical estimate with data, execution, uncertainty, benchmark, and forward limitations. |

Choose the level before [Module 21](LESSONS_04_RESEARCH.md). The [research lab protocol](RESEARCH_LAB.md) gives the full audit standard. A paid dataset or inaccessible tool is not required for levels A or B; a credible claim about historical contract-level execution requires suitable contract-level data.

title: Advanced Options Academy — complete teaching packages
body:
# Advanced Options Academy

Case seminars, analytical practice, and defended portfolio decisions. All case data are fictional unless explicitly sourced.

## Module 1: Money, markets, and the purpose of trading

Separate financial objectives, essential cash and risk capital before evaluating an option.

Stage: Foundations and account decisions. Study allocation: Four-week study reference; advance through demonstrated work. Prerequisites: Foundation diagnostic.

### Decision, intuition and learning outcome

## Begin with a decision

A budget is a set of claims on money, not merely an account balance. A dollar promised for a near-term bill cannot simultaneously absorb a speculative loss. Begin with the obligation and work toward the instrument. Percentage returns become useful only after you identify the capital base, time horizon and possible loss.

**Learning outcome:** Separate financial objectives, essential cash and risk capital before evaluating an option.

**Opening diagnostic:** Read the case brief and write the first two facts you would verify before calculating. Explain your initial intuition in three sentences, without reading the staged update or debrief. This is a baseline, not a graded claim of mastery.

**Study sequence:** Read the core teaching; reproduce one calculation without the answer; prepare the initial case memo; reveal the changed information; revise; then defend the decision and complete a fresh transfer case. The four-week reference pace can be extended when prerequisites need work.

### Core teaching and worked practice

### Lesson

Start with an everyday distinction. **Saving** puts money aside for a future need. **Investing** puts money into assets whose value and cash flows are uncertain, often for years. **Trading** means making shorter-horizon decisions to buy, sell, or hedge. None of these words describes a guaranteed return. An options position can change value much faster than a stock position, so the first trading skill is knowing which money is available for risk and which money pays for ordinary life. In your notebook, keep living expenses, emergency reserves, debt obligations, and potential trading capital as separate lines. A classroom exercise can use hypothetical capital even if you have no money available for trading.

A **share of stock** is a unit of ownership in a company. An **exchange-traded fund (ETF)** is a fund whose shares trade on an exchange and hold assets according to its rules. An **index** is a calculated measure, such as a basket's level; the index itself is not a share you can take home. Options can reference a stock, ETF, or index, but their contract terms may differ. Before learning an option, learn to ask what its underlying actually is. The [SEC's investing basics](https://www.investor.gov/introduction-investing/investing-basics/investment-products) is a starting reference for products. We will use an imaginary company, ABC, rather than a real ticker so that examples cannot be mistaken for recommendations.

Trading needs infrastructure. A **broker** is the firm through which a customer submits orders and maintains an account. An **exchange** organizes trading and publishes market rules and prices. The **Options Clearing Corporation (OCC)** clears standardized U.S. listed securities options and sets out the rights, obligations, exercise, and assignment framework in its [disclosure document](https://www.theocc.com/company-information/documents-and-archives/options-disclosure-document). The broker determines what option strategies an account is approved to use; [the SEC says approval levels and allowed strategies vary by firm](https://www.investor.gov/introduction-investing/general-resources/news-alerts/alerts-bulletins/investor-bulletins-77). You do not need an options account to complete the first part of this course.

Measure outcomes in both dollars and percentages. If 100 ABC shares cost $50 each, the position costs $5,000. At $55 each, its market value is $5,500 and its gain is $500, or `500 / 5,000 = 10%` before costs and taxes. At $45, the loss is $500, or 10%. A loss and its recovery are asymmetric: $5,000 falling by 50% becomes $2,500. A later 50% rise produces $3,750, still below the start. To return to $5,000 from $2,500 requires a 100% gain. This is why avoiding a severe loss matters more than collecting impressive small wins.

Time and alternatives matter as much as the percentage. A 10% gain over one year and a 10% gain over ten years describe different outcomes. A $500 profit from risking nearly all of a small account is different from the same profit on a well-controlled exposure. A trading journal should therefore record the starting amount, dates, capital tied up, worst loss along the way, and a sensible comparison such as holding the underlying or staying in cash. This does not mean cash is always better; it means you should be able to describe what extra risk an option is supposed to solve. The eventual aim is a repeatable decision process, not a striking single result.

A *drawdown* is a decline from a prior peak; it is not automatically the same as the total loss on one trade. Do not use a high percentage return to judge skill until you know the starting capital, risk taken, fees, and the time period.

**Common mistakes to catch:** calling an index a share, treating all account cash as available for a loss, or comparing two percentages without their time periods and drawdowns.

## Module 2: How to read an option quote

Audit a quote before converting it into an order or an expected result.

Stage: Foundations and account decisions. Study allocation: Four-week study reference; advance through demonstrated work. Prerequisites: 1.

### Decision, intuition and learning outcome

## Begin with a decision

Read a chain row like a dated contract record. The last trade answers what happened earlier; the bid and ask describe displayed interest now. Premium multiplier, exercise deliverable and displayed size answer different questions. An apparently cheap quote is not meaningful until its identity and timestamp are coherent.

**Learning outcome:** Audit a quote before converting it into an order or an expected result.

**Opening diagnostic:** Read the case brief and write the first two facts you would verify before calculating. Explain your initial intuition in three sentences, without reading the staged update or debrief. This is a baseline, not a graded claim of mastery.

**Study sequence:** Read the core teaching; reproduce one calculation without the answer; prepare the initial case memo; reveal the changed information; revise; then defend the decision and complete a fresh transfer case. The four-week reference pace can be extended when prerequisites need work.

### Core teaching and worked practice

### Lesson

A quote is an invitation to trade at indicated prices, not a record of what you will earn. The **bid** is the displayed price at which someone is currently willing to buy; the **ask** or offer is the displayed price at which someone is willing to sell. The **bid–ask spread** is the difference. If a standard 100-share stock option has a bid of $2.10 and an ask of $2.30, buying one at the displayed ask costs `$2.30 × 100 = $230`. If the market is unchanged and you immediately sell at the displayed bid, you receive `$2.10 × 100 = $210`. The $20 difference is a cost before commissions. The $2.20 **midpoint** is just `(bid + ask) / 2`; nobody has promised a fill there. Quotes can move or disappear before an order arrives.

An option quote must identify more than a ticker. Record the **underlying**, **call or put**, **strike**, **expiration**, **premium multiplier**, and **exercise deliverable** as separate fields. The premium multiplier converts a per-share quote into contract dollars; the deliverable describes what exercise transfers. They can differ on adjusted contracts. The **last trade** is a past transaction, possibly at an old price. **Volume** counts contracts traded during the session. **Open interest** counts outstanding contracts under the reporting convention and may not reflect today's trades yet. Neither volume nor open interest alone guarantees that you can enter or leave at a good price. A liquid contract often has a narrower spread and accessible size, but liquidity can change when a stock moves or news breaks. [OIC's options tools](https://www.optionseducation.org/options-quotes-calculators) show delayed quotes and calculators; delayed data are for learning, not a live execution assumption.

Consider a displayed quote: `ABC Dec 18 $50 call, bid $1.45, ask $1.65, last $1.80, volume 200, open interest 4,000`. Read it from left to right. ABC is the underlying, December 18 is the expiration, $50 is the strike, and this is a call. If the deliverable is standard 100 shares, the ask represents $165 per contract. The last price of $1.80 does **not** mean the current option can be sold for $180. At the displayed bid, one contract would bring in $145 before fees. The displayed spread is $0.20 per share, or $20 per contract. Check the quote timestamp, particularly when using free delayed data.

A **market order** asks to trade promptly against available interest and can fill at prices worse than the screen last showed. A **limit order** specifies your worst acceptable price for a buy or sale, but may never fill. Imagine a buy limit at $1.55 when the ask is $1.65. The order might be filled if someone sells at $1.55; it might also sit unfilled. The $10 improvement from ask to limit is not a saving until a fill actually occurs. In later research you will count rejected and unfilled orders as part of the process, rather than inventing midpoint trades.

The same $0.20 per-share spread has different importance for different option prices. On a $10 option it is a small fraction of the premium; on a $0.30 option it consumes most of the quoted price. Calculate both the **dollar spread** and its size relative to the ask. An option may display one contract at the best bid and many at other prices, so a larger order may not all fill at the best quote. Nor does a tight screen guarantee the same liquidity during a sudden move. As a beginner, read the chain to learn how markets work, not to identify the option with the biggest percentage movement.

**Vocabulary to own:** bid, ask, midpoint, spread, last, volume, open interest, multiplier, deliverable, market order, limit order, timestamp. Read a quote as a bundle of exact contract terms plus a time-specific market, not as a single option price.

**Common mistakes to catch:** multiplying a premium quote by 100 before checking the actual premium multiplier; assuming the share deliverable must equal that multiplier; treating a last trade as today's bid; assuming a limit order must fill; or mistaking open interest for the number of contracts traded today.

5. You cannot know tomorrow's exit price or spread from today's open interest; market conditions and quotes can change.

</details>

## Module 3: Calls, puts, buyers, and sellers

Distinguish moneyness, payoff and profit for buyers and writers.

Stage: Foundations and account decisions. Study allocation: Four-week study reference; advance through demonstrated work. Prerequisites: 2.

### Decision, intuition and learning outcome

## Begin with a decision

An option can finish in the money while its owner loses money. Intrinsic value measures the exercise payoff; profit also includes the premium paid or received and costs. Write separate cash-flow lines before saying that a directional prediction was correct.

**Learning outcome:** Distinguish moneyness, payoff and profit for buyers and writers.

**Opening diagnostic:** Read the case brief and write the first two facts you would verify before calculating. Explain your initial intuition in three sentences, without reading the staged update or debrief. This is a baseline, not a graded claim of mastery.

**Study sequence:** Read the core teaching; reproduce one calculation without the answer; prepare the initial case memo; reveal the changed information; revise; then defend the decision and complete a fresh transfer case. The four-week reference pace can be extended when prerequisites need work.

### Core teaching and worked practice

### Lesson

An option is a contract with two sides. The **buyer** or *holder* pays a premium for a right. The **seller** or *writer* receives that premium when opening a short position and accepts an obligation if assigned. For the standard stock options in this chapter, one contract covers 100 shares. A **call** buyer may buy those shares at the strike; a **put** buyer may sell them at the strike. The call writer may have to sell or deliver shares, and the put writer may have to buy them. These rights and obligations are described in the [SEC options bulletin](https://www.investor.gov/introduction-investing/general-resources/news-alerts/alerts-bulletins/investor-bulletins-63) and [OCC disclosure document](https://www.theocc.com/company-information/documents-and-archives/options-disclosure-document).

To learn option arithmetic, hold time still and imagine the moment of expiration. A call's **intrinsic value** per share is `max(stock price − strike, 0)`. A put's is `max(strike − stock price, 0)`. The `max(..., 0)` part says the holder need not exercise a right that has no favorable intrinsic value. **Profit** then subtracts the premium paid by a buyer or adds the premium received by a writer. Before expiration, an option can have **extrinsic value** on top of intrinsic value because time and uncertain future moves still matter. So an expiration break-even price is neither a forecast nor the price where you must sell before expiration.

Work through a call slowly. ABC is $100 today. You pay $3 per share for one $105 call: `$3 × 100 = $300` leaves your account. If ABC ends at $112, the right to buy at $105 is worth `$7 × 100 = $700`; subtract $300 and your expiration profit is $400 before fees. If ABC ends at $106, the right is worth $100 and the profit is **negative $200**. A correct prediction that the stock would rise was not enough. The expiration break-even is `$105 + $3 = $108`. Below the strike the call's intrinsic value is zero and the premium can be lost in full. A put works in the opposite stock direction: a $95 put costing $2 has a $93 expiration break-even. At a stock price of $88, it is worth `$7 × 100 = $700`, leaving $500 after its $200 premium.

Now reverse the position. If someone **writes an uncovered $105 call** for $3, $300 is the most premium they can keep from that call. At $112 expiration, the intrinsic obligation is $700, producing `+$300 − $700 = −$400` before fees. If the stock rose to $200, the obligation would be far larger; because a stock has no fixed upper price ceiling, the uncovered call has no fixed theoretical loss ceiling. A **short $95 put** sold for $2 can require buying 100 shares for $9,500 even if the shares have collapsed. If the stock went to zero, its expiration loss would be `$9,500 − $200 = $9,300` before fees. Receiving premium therefore does not make a position low risk or turn it into a salary.

You will also hear **in the money** and **out of the money**. A call is in the money when the stock is above its strike; a put is in the money when the stock is below its strike. This says only whether exercise has immediate intrinsic value. It does **not** say whether the original buyer has made a profit. For example, the $105 call at stock $106 is in the money by $1 per share but still loses $2 per share after its $3 purchase premium. Before expiration, a call might trade above its intrinsic value because time remains. If the $105 call is quoted at $7 while the stock is $110, $5 is intrinsic and $2 is extrinsic in that illustrative quote. The actual quote can change for many reasons. At expiration, that extra time value disappears from the simple payoff model.

**Vocabulary to own:** holder, writer, long, short, strike, premium, intrinsic, extrinsic, in the money, out of the money, expiration break-even, obligation. The words *long* and *short* refer to owning and writing the option, not automatically to optimism or pessimism about the stock. A short put, for example, often benefits when a stock stays up, yet it can lose heavily when the stock falls.

**Common mistakes to catch:** calling an in-the-money option profitable without subtracting the premium, assuming a writer's premium is the maximum possible loss, or using an expiration break-even as a price forecast.
